title: Invocation
en:
In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Ever-Merciful.

We praise You, in whose hand is the dominion of everything and through whom it is sustained; from whom every living thing takes its beginning and to whom it returns. From the leaves of the celestial spheres are recited the signs of His oneness and praise, and throughout the horizons and within souls appear the testimonies to His holiness and glory. No leaf falls within the created worlds without His resplendent wisdom knowing it; no order of being exists within the realm of possibility without His all-subduing power encompassing it. His uniquely one essence is exalted above likenesses and equals, and His beginningless and everlasting attributes are free from passing away and extinction. The brows of the heavenly bodies bow before the might of His majesty, and the lips of the holy lights speak in gratitude for His bounty.

title: Thanksgiving
en: We thank You for teaching us the foundations of religious doctrines, bestowing upon us the gifts of certain knowledge, guiding us to the path of salvation and the way of right direction, and showing us the courses of uprightness and the road of soundness.

title: Blessing upon the Prophet
en: We invoke blessings upon Your prophet Muḥammad, endowed with the noblest traits of character and sent as a mercy to created beings. You sent him when the landmarks of guidance had been effaced and the banners of ruin had appeared, when the path of truth had been obliterated and its traces erased, and the lamps of truthfulness were on the verge of going out. He raised religion’s landmarks and certainty’s distinguishing signs, made clear the path of demonstration and the evidence of faith, established truth’s proof, and illuminated the clear road of the revealed law. Thus breasts opened to the light of clear proofs, the rust of specious objections was removed from hearts, the face of the days grew bright, the affairs of Islam were set in order, and humankind held fast to the firmest bond, which cannot be broken.

title: Blessing upon the family and Companions
en: And upon his family and Companions: the successors who uphold religion and the allies of certainty; the lamps of the nations and the keys to generosity; the treasuries of knowledge and the emblems of wisdom; the leaders of the precincts of holiness and the great ones of the places of intimacy. They climbed the summits of realities with the steps of thought and illuminated the seven paths with the lights of transmitted teachings. They fought for religion and dispelled its calamities and afflictions; they hastened toward certainty and turned away from it assaults and misfortunes. Then Islam’s mouth smiled, the affairs of the Muslims were ordered and made clear, and—by God’s promise and as a right He has taken upon Himself—the believers received support.

title: The author’s earlier scholarly life
en: To proceed: in my early days and the prime of my life, when living was fresh and youth retained its bloom, when the branch of early manhood was still growing, the full moons of hope rose radiant, and the faces of my circumstances smiled with gladness; when the habitations of excellence were flourishing in their precincts and courtyards, and the gardens of knowledge were watered in their buds and flowers—I ranged in thought through the sciences, seeking their flowers and lights, and expounded books in the various disciplines, lifting their veils to disclose their secrets. The accomplished came to me from distant regions to dive for the unique pearls of their benefits, and the discerning repeatedly visited me to seek their elusive rewards. They knew that we had expended our powers in acquiring subtle points and exhausted our intellects in the pursuit of realities.

title: The demand for a work of kalām
en: When they saw that the science of kalām—the foundation of revealed laws and rulings, and the measure of the principles of Islamic doctrines—was the most precious object of aspiration and ascent, and the most important destination at which the mounts of inquiry could kneel, they all circled around its pursuit. For it is the most firmly built of the sciences, the truest in exposition, the noblest in results, the brightest in illumination, the soundest in proof and evidence, and the clearest in road and path. They sought a way into its presence, a lamp upon its domes, and a key to open its gate. I therefore seized a gleam within the darkness of time and a respite from the fangs of calamities; I took advantage of an opening in time’s watchfulness and a moment of relief from the press of disturbances.

title: The compendium and its commentary
en: I began composing a compendium entitled al-Maqāṣid, arranging within it choice rarities and pearls of useful learning, together with a commentary that expands its concise statements, solves its riddles, unfolds its compressed discussions, and clarifies its difficulties. It establishes the matters sought in accordance with what is required, examines their critical points with an uncommon precision, formulates the questions to the extent intended without excess, and sets out the proofs so that they are neither countered nor ensnared. Its expressions open ears and expand breasts, and cause mountains and rocks to split open with rivers and flowers. Its meanings make the faces of pages beam and the mouths of lines smile, shining through the discourse as though they were light upon light.

title: The priority of revealed matters
en: I have devoted my effort to including discussions neglected by later theologians but treated with great care by the exacting scholars among their predecessors—especially matters known through revelation (السمعيات). These are the highest object of inquiry and the ultimate aim within the foundations of religion, the firmest bond and the chief support for the people of truth and certainty.

title: The first circulation of the work
en: Once I had drafted part of the book and portions of its chapters and divisions, students hastened to it and it passed from hand to hand among people of understanding. Every seeker directed his quest toward it; every aspirant attached his desire to it. Every newcomer sought the light of its fire, and every explorer turned his resolve toward it. They began praising it, proposing further requests, and striking the flint of the desire for more.

title: Frustration and the decline of learning
en: Meanwhile I expended my effort, but what I wanted withdrew; the intended goal lagged behind attainment and turned aside. The days obstructed and prevented, promising without fulfilling. Time called forth complaint and lamentation, and the intellect laughed and wept. How astonishing were the dwindling and corruption of men’s aspirations, the retreat and stagnation of the market of excellences, the weakening of truth’s structure and the collapse of its pillars, the growth of falsehood and the persistence of its tyranny! The days lengthened, filled with anger and reproach, joining forces against the intellect. They joined eyelids to sleeplessness and separated eyes from repose. Speech had no scope, attainment no support; the archers’ bows had no draw, and the arrow of contest no true aim—and so it went on.

title: Displacement and loss
en: At last my age struck me with what it struck me, and events afflicted me with what they inflicted. Circumstances stood between me and security—indeed, between me and my hopes. My condition became [the pouring out of the buckets of my worn waterskins: the wording and image require verification]. Homelands and cherished aims receded from me; regions and journeys cast me far afield. I endured circumstances that would turn forelocks white and terrors that would melt firmly rooted mountains. I witnessed causes of the extinction of the sciences, the diminution of their resources and the disruption of their supports, at which breath almost failed and mountains almost split. They were seized by desolation and bewilderment [the exact descriptive wording is uncertain], and I stood at the pass of farewell: no traces of dwellings, no inhabited places, no vestiges, no homes.

title: Repeated interruptions
en: Whenever I intended to unfold what I had folded away, and set myself to complete it or wished to do so, hindrances and interruptions arose, and calamities and disturbances occurred. Even the slightest of them would come between a person and his own heart and tarnish the mirror of his thought and intellect. The least of them would remove the freshness of his mind and vision and take away the lustre of his inward and outward condition.

title: Resumption and completion
en: Then a favour from my Lord overtook me, and a returning measure of understanding and intellect sustained me. I turned to completing the book and ordering those chapters and divisions. Praise be to God, it emerged as a buried treasury of rare jewels and an ocean laden with precious benefits, containing subtle insights long kept in store and protected from loss. Its discourse is refined and its intention made clear through expositions that bring repose to the souls of serious students, dispel the specious objections of those who advance falsehood, illuminate seekers’ hearts with their lights, and kindle their fires over the hearts of the envious. Only the learned comprehend its clear proofs, and only wrongdoers deny its signs. The scholars of the lands are stirred by it in every assembly; none belittles it except one wandering aimlessly through some valley. Whomever God guides is rightly guided, and whomever He leaves astray has no guide.

title: An appeal to the reader
en: If something reaches your ears that you have not heard from earlier scholars, do not be hasty: pause as a reflective person pauses. Perhaps, through a flash of divine lightning and the radiance of a lordly light, from the right bank of the valley in the blessed place, you will discover a clear demonstration for it, or an explanation from others [the concluding words are textually uncertain]. God—glorified and exalted—is the patron of assistance and success, and worthy to fulfil the hopes of the believers.

title: The theoretical and practical powers
en: I say: Know that a human being has a theoretical power (قوة نظرية), whose perfection is to know realities as they are, and a practical power (قوة عملية), whose perfection is to conduct affairs as they ought to be conducted, thereby attaining happiness in both abodes. Revealed religion and philosophy agree in attending to the perfection of human souls in these two powers and in facilitating the path to these two ends. Yet rational inquiry follows its guidance within revealed religion, and its inclination within philosophy.

title: Kalām and the division of theoretical philosophy
en: Just as the philosophical sages committed theoretical and practical wisdom to writing to help people acquire the perfections associated with the two powers, so the great figures of revealed religion and the scholars of the community committed to writing the science of kalām and the science of revealed laws and rulings. Kalām thus occupies within revealed religion the place occupied by theoretical wisdom within philosophy. According to the philosophers, theoretical wisdom divides into knowledge concerning things independent of matter both in existence and in conception—metaphysics (الإلهي); things independent of matter only in conception—mathematics (الرياضي); and things that are not independent of matter in either respect—natural philosophy (الطبيعي).

title: The beginning and the return
en: Each of these has many divisions and branches. Nevertheless, what takes priority in consideration, according to the testimony of reason and transmission, is knowledge of the beginning and the return (المبدأ والمعاد), indicated by faith in God Most High and the Last Day. The way to reach this knowledge is rational investigation (النظر) of contingent beings—substances (جواهر) and accidents (أعراض)—as passages of God’s Book direct us.

title: The ends of human perfection
en: How well the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī—may God honour his face—indicated that what matters in the perfection of the practical power is that by which life in this world is ordered and salvation in the return is attained; and, in the theoretical power, knowledge of the beginning, the return, and what lies between them, through rational inquiry and reflection. He said: “May God have mercy upon one who makes provision for himself, prepares for his grave, and knows whence he comes, where he is, and whither he goes.”

title: The five substantive fields
en: Accordingly, the scholars of revealed religion confined their attention to what concerns knowledge of the Maker, His attributes and His acts, and what follows from that: prophecy, the return, and the other matters to which reason has no access on its own. They also considered the states upon which the establishment of those matters depends, whether peculiar to substances and accidents or common to most existents. Thus the substantive divisions of kalām became five: general matters (الأمور العامة), accidents, substances, divine matters (الإلهيات), and matters known through revelation (السمعيات).

title: Why there are six divisions, in this order
en: It has become customary to precede these with discussions serving as preliminaries, called principles (المبادئ). We have therefore arranged the book in six principal divisions. The classification works as follows. If a discussion belongs to the substantive aims of kalām, it concerns either matters known through revelation—the sixth division—or rational matters. A rational discussion is either peculiar to the Necessary Existent—the fifth; to a contingent substance—the fourth; to an accident—the third; or peculiar to none of these—the second. If it does not belong to the substantive aims of the discipline, it falls within the book’s first division. The reason for this order is that later discussions depend upon earlier ones for certain demonstrations. Classification and appropriateness may nevertheless require placing a discussion among matters treated elsewhere: for example, the question of the vision of God among divine matters, and the restoration of what has ceased to exist among matters known through revelation.

title: Why the principles occupy three chapters
en: I say: He arranged it in three chapters because some principles are those with which scholars consider every science should begin: knowledge of its definition, subject matter, end, and the like. He called these “preliminaries” and assigned them a chapter. Others are those with which they specifically prefaced kalām, such as the discussions of knowledge and rational investigation. The acquisition of doctrines through rational investigation and inference, and the refutation of those who deny that knowledge is attained at all, or that it is gained from rational investigation either absolutely or specifically in divine matters, depend upon these discussions. No Islamic science is more appropriate for explaining them, so he assigned them two chapters.

en: He says: “Kalām is knowledge of religious doctrines derived from certain proofs.”

title: Possessing a quality and conceiving it
en: I say: Qualities of the soul may occur in it either as the qualities themselves—in which case the soul is qualified by them—or through their forms—in which case it conceives them. A generous person possesses generosity even if he does not conceive it, while someone who is not generous may conceive generosity without possessing it.

title: Why a science needs a definition
en: It is evident that the reality of every science, kalām and otherwise, consists in numerous conceptions (تصورات) and assents (تصديقات), whose actual acquisition is sought through rational investigation and inference. Something is therefore needed that provides an overall conception coextensive with them, protecting inquiry from omitting what belongs to the science or becoming occupied with what does not. This is what is meant by defining a science, and so definition belongs among its preliminaries. Such definitions have often been omitted, particularly in the religious and literary sciences, because it became customary to set down a science’s questions and proofs, explain the associated conceptions, and then acquire the science in that form by learning from a teacher or understanding a book.

title: The formation of the religious sciences
en: With this established, we say: some judgements attributed to the revealed law concern action and are called derivative and practical; others concern belief and are called foundational and doctrinal. The earliest scholars, through the blessing of companionship with the Prophet—God bless him and grant him peace—their proximity to his time, hearing reports from him, and witnessing their traces, had no need to set down these judgements, arrange them in chapters and divisions, or multiply questions of branches and foundations. Occurrences and disagreements were few, and trustworthy authorities could readily be consulted. Eventually opinions diverged, inclinations toward innovations and partisan desires appeared, legal responses and cases multiplied, and a need arose for further inquiry and attention. Those skilled in rational investigation and inference then began deriving rulings, expended their efforts in establishing the doctrines of Islam, and turned to laying out their foundations and governing principles, presenting their arguments and demonstrations concisely, and recording questions with their proofs and specious objections with their answers.

title: Fiqh, the greater fiqh, and the name kalām
en: They called knowledge of these matters fiqh, and reserved the name “the greater fiqh” (الفقه الأكبر) for doctrinal matters. Most reserved fiqh for practical matters and called doctrinal inquiry “the science of divine unity and attributes”, naming it after its best-known and noblest parts. title: Certainty and the scope of religious doctrine
en: They required certainty in its proofs because probabilistic judgement (ظن) carries no authority in doctrinal matters, but does so in practical matters. It is therefore clear that kalām is knowledge of the doctrinal principles of the revealed law acquired from their certain proofs. This is what “religious doctrines” means: doctrines attributed to Muḥammad’s religion—God bless him and grant him peace—whether or not their establishment depends upon revelation, and whether or not they actually belong to that religion: as with the kalām of the people of truth in the first case, and that of their opponents in the second. Our definition, “knowledge of religious doctrines derived from certain proofs”, thus corresponds to their definition of fiqh as “knowledge of the derivative rulings of the revealed law derived from their particular proofs”. It also agrees with what is transmitted from one of the religion’s great authorities: fiqh is the soul’s knowledge of what is in its favour and what is incumbent upon it, and the part concerning doctrines is the greater fiqh.

title: What the definition includes and excludes
en: The definition excludes knowledge of non-religious matters, knowledge of derivative religious rulings, God Most High’s knowledge, the Messenger’s knowledge of doctrines—God bless him and grant him peace—and the belief of the uncritical follower, on the view that calls it knowledge. This is what we intend by “knowledge of doctrines derived from proofs”.

title: The subject matter and unity of a science
en:
**He says:** “Its subject matter is the known.”

**I say:** The scholars agree that sciences differ in themselves according to the difference of their subject matters. It is therefore appropriate to begin a science by stating its subject matter: this explains what distinguishes it in itself, after its definition has explained what distinguishes it conceptually. Moreover, knowing the respect that unifies the multiplicity sought provides a general grasp of that multiplicity. When one seeks to acquire its details, one's inquiry will then remain directed toward what belongs to it rather than toward what does not. The primary and intrinsic respect unifying a science's questions is undoubtedly its subject matter: they share it and are united through it, as we shall explain.

The precise account is this. When scholars sought to know the conditions of things to the extent of human capacity—this being what is meant by wisdom—they took realities, whether species, genera or otherwise, such as human being, animal and existent, and investigated the conditions proper to them, establishing these by proofs. They thus obtained acquired propositions whose predicates are the essential attributes of those realities; these they called “questions.” Every group of propositions referring to one of those things, whose subjects are that thing itself, a part of it, a species of it or an essential attribute of it, they made into a particular science, separately written down, named and taught. They did so because, despite the propositions' multiplicity and the diversity of their predicates, this group possesses unity through its subject matter—that is, through sharing it in the manner just stated.

The group may also possess unity in other respects, such as benefit or end. From one such respect an account is drawn that makes it conceivable generally and as a unity. If this account indicates the reality of what its name signifies, namely that mentally constituted composite, it is a definition: for example, “a science investigating such-and-such,” or “knowledge of such-and-such rules.” Otherwise it is a description: for example, “a science through which one becomes capable of such-and-such,” “avoids such-and-such,” or “possesses an instrument for such-and-such.”

It is therefore clear that the subject matter is what unifies the questions of one science considered in themselves, even if other respects accrue to them, such as definition and end. To say “this is one science and that another” means only that the former investigates the conditions of one thing and the latter those of another, differing from it either intrinsically or in the respect under consideration. Sciences therefore differ in themselves, considered in their own constitution, only according to their subject matters, although a learner may distinguish them through their definitions, ends and the like.

title: Difference, affinity and inclusion among sciences
en:
For this reason, scholars also determine the mutual separation, affinity and inclusion of sciences by their subject matters. If one science's subject matter is wholly distinct from another's, the sciences are completely separate. If it is more general, the sciences stand in a relation of inclusion. If their subjects are intrinsically one thing considered in different respects, or two things sharing a genus or something else, the sciences have an affinity, according to distinctions explained in their appropriate place.

In general, scholars agree that one thing cannot be the subject matter of two sciences without some difference of consideration: it must be taken without qualification in one and with a qualification in the other, or with a different qualification in each. Nor can two things be the subject matter of one science unless their unity in a genus, end or something else is considered. Without this, the unity and difference of sciences have no meaning.

One cannot object: “Knowledge differs according to what is known, namely the questions. Just as questions differ through their subjects, they differ through their predicates. Why not make predicates the basis of distinction, so that investigation of some essential attributes constitutes one science and investigation of others another, although the subject matter is the same? This is more appropriate: the subject is like matter, from which genus is taken, while essential attributes are like form, from which the differentia effecting complete distinction is taken.”

We answer: unity and difference would then have no determinate measure, and each science would become a multitude of sciences, since it necessarily includes many kinds of essential attributes. Arithmetic, for example, would become many sciences according to its different predicates: even, odd, evenly even, oddly even and so forth. The same would hold of the other sciences. The error arises from failing to distinguish “knowledge” in the sense of a discipline—the whole body of investigations concerning a subject matter—from “knowledge” in the sense of a form's occurrence [in cognition]. If the latter were intended, each question would be a separate item of knowledge.

Furthermore, the basis of unity and difference, and of the separation, affinity and inclusion that follow them, must be something determinate, evident or explained. That is the subject matter. Essential attributes have no fixed enumeration or exhaustive limit: everyone may establish as many as he can, and they become manifest through their establishment within the science itself. Their definitions at the beginning of a science are therefore nominal definitions, which may become real definitions once the attributes have been established. The definitions of the subject matter and its parts, by contrast, are real definitions.

As for the claim about matter and form, it is false. Subject and predicate are both material parts of a proposition; its formal element is the judgement. Moreover, our discussion concerns not an individual question but the mentally constituted composite that is the science. The questions plainly constitute its matter, while its form comes back to their unifying respect: through this, the questions become that particular discipline.

title: Why a common genus does not automatically make one science
en:
If you say: “Requiring the subjects of one science to share a genus or something else does not remove the difficulty about scientific unity and difference. The subjects of two sciences almost always share something essential or accidental—existence at least. Arithmetic and geometry, for instance, investigate number and magnitude, which fall under one genus, quantity. Yet they are treated as two sciences of equal rank, whereas grammar, investigating the kinds of word, is treated as one.”

I answer: if things are investigated precisely in the respect in which they share that common feature, the science is one. The test is whether it investigates everything sharing that feature. Otherwise the sciences are several. Do you not see that arithmetic and geometry do not investigate time, although it is a kind of quantity? This is the point of the statement in the *Shifāʾ* that arithmetic and geometry are each made a separate science because each investigates what accrues to its subject matter as such: number in arithmetic and magnitude in geometry. If they investigated them insofar as they are quantities, the subject matter of each would be quantity, or the two sciences would be one. If each investigated its subject matter insofar as it is existent, they would not be distinct from first philosophy.

title: Four different senses of introducing the subject matter
en:
If you say: “Scholars explicitly make the subject matter a preliminary, a separate component of the science, and one of its conceptual principles. How can this be?”

I answer: their intention is that assent to the existence of the subject itself—number in arithmetic, for example—is a component of the science. Their stated reason shows this: how can one seek to establish something of what is not known to be established? Conceiving the subject belongs to the conceptual principles; assenting that it is the subject matter belongs to the preliminaries. Conceiving the concept of ‘subject matter,’ namely that whose essential attributes are investigated, belongs to the logical discipline of demonstration. These are four matters that can be confused.

They did not classify assent to the subject's existence among the principles of assent, although they classified its conception among the conceptual principles, because by the former they meant premises from which the science's syllogisms are composed. They did not classify assent that it is the subject matter among the material components because this is fully established only after the science is complete; it resembles the science's fruits more than its components. For example, our statement “number is the subject matter of arithmetic because arithmetic investigates only its essential attributes” is established only after a comprehensive grasp of arithmetic. Assent to its being the subject matter thus precedes the science in a general way but follows it in verified detail.

It should be understood that these requirements concern theoretical demonstrative disciplines. In others they may be apparent, as in jurisprudence and its principles, or apparent only with some forcing, as in certain literary disciplines. A discipline may consist of several conventions, technical usages and reminders concerning one thing, without establishing a subject's essential attributes by proofs built from premises. We have discussed these matters at length, although they are evident from the standpoint of the discipline of demonstration, because doubts have entered them since the principles of the five [logical] disciplines fell out of use.

title: Why kalām takes the known as its subject matter
en:
Once this is established, we say: the subject matter of kalām is the known insofar as establishing religious doctrines is connected with it. Kalām investigates the Maker's conditions, such as beginninglessness, unity, power and will; and the conditions of body and accident, such as temporal origination, dependence, composition from parts and susceptibility to annihilation. These are either Islamic doctrines or means to them. All this investigates conditions of the known.

Like “existent,” “known” is evident in its establishedness and encompasses the subject matters of the other Islamic sciences, so kalām stands above them all. “Known” is preferred to “existent,” however, so that the account remains valid for someone who rejects mental existence, does not explain knowledge as a form's occurrence in the intellect, and regards investigations of the nonexistent and the ontological state as questions of kalām.

If it is said: “If ‘known’ or ‘existent’ means its concept, many—indeed most—predicates of the questions are narrower than it. If it means what bears that concept, the predicates are broader: for example, the Maker's visibility, the beginninglessness of His speech and the temporal origination of body. Everyone agrees that a narrower predicate cannot be an essential attribute, and that a broader predicate is not employed in its full generality. Equality, for example, accrues to number through quantity but is used in arithmetic only after restriction to numerical equality. The dispute is merely whether it is called an essential attribute before that restriction.”

We answer: the required restriction concerns the science's subject matter, not the subject of each question, whether [the relevant attribute covers it] without qualification or together with its opposite, as number is never without either evenness or oddness. Do you not see that ‘even’ is predicated of the product of an odd number and an even number although it is broader than that product? The *Shifāʾ* says that an essential attribute may be coextensive with the subject, as the equality of a triangle's three angles to two right angles; absolutely narrower, as evenness in relation to number; or narrower in one respect, as equality in relation to number. Equality is an essential attribute of number because number's genus, quantity, enters its definition. The two may occur together, number may occur without equality—as is evident—and equality may occur without number, as in magnitudes. An essential attribute may also be absolutely broader than the subject, as evenness in relation to the product of an odd number and an even number.

title: The questions, end and benefit of kalām
en:
**He says:** “Its questions are the theoretical propositions of revealed religion concerning belief.”

**I say:** A general conception of a science's questions is sometimes made one of its preliminaries because it further distinguishes the science. ‘Theoretical’ qualifies the propositions because everyone agrees that what is self-evident is not one of the questions and sought conclusions of a science. A question means precisely something asked about and sought through a proof. A self-evident judgement may nevertheless be introduced among the questions in order to explain why it is true. In that respect it is acquired, rather than self-evident. A discipline may also consist of conventions, technical usages and evident judgements requiring reminders, and these may be its questions. This is how the statement in the *Tajrīd* on logic should be understood: questions are what is demonstrated in a science, if they are not evident.

**He says:** “Its end…”

What a thing leads to, and what results from it, is called its “end” in that respect; insofar as it is sought through action, it is called a “purpose.” If it is something everyone naturally desires, it is called a “benefit.” A science begins by mentioning its end so the learner knows whether it accords with his purpose and so his investigation is neither pointless nor misdirected. Its benefit is mentioned to increase his diligence and enthusiasm.

The end of kalām is that faith and assent to the judgements of revealed religion should become certain and firmly established, unshaken by the specious arguments of those who promote falsehood. Its worldly benefit is the ordering of livelihood through maintaining justice and the dealings needed for the continuation of the species, in a manner that does not lead to corruption. title: The rank of kalām
en:
**He says:** “It is therefore the noblest of the sciences.”

**I say:** Its subject matter has been shown to be the highest of subject matters, what it knows the most exalted of known things, and its end the noblest of ends. There has also been an indication of the great need for it, the dependence of the other religious sciences upon it, and the reliability of its proofs: they are certainties upon which reason and revelation agree. It is therefore clear that it is the noblest science, for these are the grounds of a science's nobility.

The criticisms of it transmitted from the early generations concern cases in which it is pursued to promote religious partisanship, corrupt beginners' beliefs, or entangle them in the valleys of error by making the philosophers' doctrines attractive.

title: Earlier accounts: the existent under the governing principles of Islam
en:
**He says:** “The earlier scholars…”

**I say:** These discussions, although connected with the subject matter, have been postponed to preserve the orderly exposition of subject matter, questions and end. Earlier scholars of kalām made its subject matter the existent insofar as it is existent, because its investigations return to that.

As the Imām, the Proof of Islam, says: the theologian considers the most general of things, the existent, and divides it into beginningless and temporally originated. He divides the temporally originated into substance and accident, and accident into what requires life—such as knowledge and power—and what does not, such as colour and taste. He divides substance into animal, plant and inanimate thing, and explains whether their differences concern species or accidents. He considers the beginningless and shows that it is neither multiple nor composite and is distinguished from the originated by attributes necessary for it, matters impossible for it, and judgements possible of it without necessity or impossibility. He explains that acting is possible for it and that the world is its possible act, which therefore requires an originator; that it has power to send messengers and disclose their truthfulness through miracles; and that this has actually occurred. At this point reason's independent activity reaches its limit, and one begins receiving from the Prophet—whose truthfulness has been established—and accepting what he says concerning God, the beginning and the return.

Since the subject matter of divine science in philosophy is the existent insofar as it is existent, and sciences differ through their subject matters, “existent” is qualified here by its being connected with investigations conducted according to the governing principles of Islam. Kalām is thus distinguished from philosophical divine science because its investigation proceeds according to those principles: the familiar way called religion and religious law, and the rules known with certainty from the Book, the Sunna and consensus. Examples include the One producing many things, an angel descending from heaven, the world's being preceded by nonexistence and ceasing after existence, and other rules held certain in Islam but not in philosophy.

This is the meaning of the statement that this science rests upon adherence to the Book and Sunna: its investigations are connected with them, attributed to them and conducted according to their rules, as implied by attributing the doctrines to religion. It is also said that the “governing principles of Islam” mean its foundations: the Book, the Sunna, consensus and rational considerations that do not contradict them.

In sum, the point is to preserve the rules of revealed religion throughout the investigations and not contradict its certainties by following what deficient human intellects conclude, as philosophy's procedure does. It does not mean that every investigation must in fact be true and authentically attributable to Islam; otherwise the definition would not include the kalām of the corporealists, Muʿtazilites, Khārijites and comparable groups.

Consequently, the following objection does not apply: “The governing principles of Islam are the true questions of kalām. If truth and attribution to Islam mean actual truth and attribution, this restriction cannot distinguish kalām, since it is not an evident concomitant: theologians and others alike claim their doctrines are true. Nor would the definition include opponents' kalām, many of whose principles are false, although it is admittedly kalām. If truth means truth according to the investigator's belief, whether correct or mistaken, the restriction fails to distinguish kalām from divine science, since both share this.”

title: Nonexistents, states and mental existence
en:
**He says:** “If it is said…”

**I say:** The *Mawāqif* objects to making the existent as such the subject matter of kalām: kalām sometimes investigates conditions of what is not considered under the aspect of existence, although it exists, such as investigation and proof; and conditions of what has no existence at all, such as the nonexistent and the ontological state. Nor can “existent” be taken to include both mental and external existence so as to encompass everything, since theologians do not affirm mental existence.

The answer is that we do not concede that these discussions are questions of kalām. Investigation and proof belong to its principles, as we explained. Discussions of the nonexistent and the state are supplements to the question of existence: they clarify and complete the intended account by considering its opposites.

One cannot object that restoring the nonexistent, the impossibility of infinite regress, the rejection of prime matter and similar discussions are unquestionably questions. We answer that these concern conditions of the existent: whether it can be restored after nonexistence, whether it can extend in an infinite series, and whether body is composed of prime matter and form.

Even if these are conceded to be questions, your objection applies only if “existent as such” means externally existent on condition that its existence is considered. That is not the intention. It means existent without qualification, whether mental or external, necessary or contingent, substance or accident, and so forth. Investigation and proof concern conditions of actual existence, even when that existence is not explicitly considered; the remaining cases concern mental existence. Many theologians affirm mental existence, as their own statements expressly show. Anyone who does not must turn instead to “the known.”

title: God alone, or God and dependent beings, as subject matter
en:
**He says:** “It has also been said…”

**I say:** Among later scholars, the judge al-Urmawī held that kalām's subject matter is God's essence. It investigates His affirmative and negative attributes, and His acts concerning this world—for example, how the world proceeds from Him through choice, its temporal origination, the creation of acts and the ordering of the world, as in the study of prophethoods and their consequences—or concerning the hereafter, as in resurrection and the other matters known through revelation. Kalām would thus be the science investigating the Maker's conditions: His affirmative and negative attributes and His acts concerning this world and the hereafter.

The author of the *Ṣaḥāʾif* followed him, but added to this: the subject matter is God's essence considered in itself, and contingent beings considered in their dependence upon God. Kalām investigates essential attributes of God's essence as such and essential attributes of contingent beings insofar as they need Him. Their unifying respect is the existent. It would thus be the science investigating the Maker's conditions and the conditions of contingent beings insofar as they need Him, according to the governing principles of Islam.

This should be the meaning of his statement: “the science investigating God's essence and attributes and the conditions of contingent beings in the beginning and the return according to the governing principles of Islam.” Otherwise, investigating the subject matter itself has no meaning. He nevertheless answers that “God's essence” in the definition means the essence considered through attributes—for example, the essence as noncomposite and as neither substance nor accident. Investigating it in this respect belongs to the questions, like investigating the attributes themselves. The subject matter is the essence as such, which is not investigated within the science. This suggests that the predicate in “the Necessary is neither substance nor accident” is God's essence considered under the absence of substantiality and accidentality.

title: Why broader philosophical discussions enter kalām
en:
If it is said: “If the subject matter were God's essence alone, or together with contingent essences insofar as they depend upon Him, the questions would investigate only their conditions. Yet many discussions of general matters, substances and accidents concern contingent beings without considering their dependence upon the Necessary.”

We answer: such discussions may be digressions intended to complete the discipline by mentioning, alongside the principal object, related supplements, ramifications, opposites and similar matters: for example, the nonexistent, the state, and the divisions of quiddity, motions and bodies. They may report opponents' positions in order to refute them, as in discussions of the cause of certainty, atmospheric phenomena and separate immaterial substances. Or they may serve as principles upon which some questions depend, introduced to establish the intended conclusion without leaving its proof dependent upon something unexplained: for example, the commonality of existence, the impossibility of infinite regress, the possibility of one thing being both recipient and agent, the possibility of a void and the finitude of dimensions.

Anything beyond this is superfluous discussion intended to increase the number of investigations, as has become common among later scholars who mix many questions of natural philosophy and mathematics into kalām.

If it is said: “Kalām cannot have principles needing explanation and demonstration. A science's principles are explained only in a higher science, and no religious science stands above kalām: all are particular relative to it and ultimately depend upon it. Its principles must therefore be self-evident.”

We answer: a science explaining the principles of a religious science need be neither higher nor itself religious. It is agreed that legal theory draws upon Arabic linguistic science and that some of its principles are established there.

title: Where a science's principles are established
en:
The detailed account, as stated in the *Shifāʾ* and elsewhere, is that a science's principles may be self-evident and therefore established in no science. If not self-evident, they may be established in a higher science because their standing is too elevated for treatment in the lower one. “Body is composed of prime matter and form,” for example, is a principle of natural philosophy but a question of first philosophy. Alternatively, they may be established in a lower science because their standing is too low for treatment in the higher one. The impossibility of an indivisible part, for example, is a question of natural philosophy but a principle of divine science used to establish prime matter and form. It must be established through premises whose validity does not depend on them, lest there be circularity.

A principle may also be established in the very science concerned, provided that it is not a principle of all its questions and is not established by a question depending on it, again to avoid circularity. It is then a principle in one respect and a question in another. Most geometrical questions are like this. Likewise, “a command signifies obligation” is a question of legal theory and a principle of the question establishing the obligation of analogy by appeal to God's words, “So take heed” [Q 59:2].

In this last case the investigation must concern the conditions of the discipline's subject matter, if it is to count among its questions. Our present case—the conditions of contingent beings without consideration of their dependence—is not of this kind. They must therefore be explained in a lower or higher science. Such a principle is established by a certain proof consistent with religious rules, even if the science is not counted among the Islamic sciences, as with divine science investigating the conditions of the existent without qualification.

There is another point. The commentary on the *Ṣaḥāʾif* suggests that investigating contingent beings' conditions under the aspect of dependence does not require explicit consideration of that dependence in every question. Rather, it means investigating conditions that accrue to contingent beings because of their dependence upon God. The conditions investigated in kalām are specific conditions known as flowing from the operation of God's power. That occurs only because contingent beings need Him; these conditions therefore accrue to them through their need of Him.

title: Can God's existence be established if God is the subject matter?
en:
**He says:** “It has been objected…”

**I say:** Some philosophical discussions do not undermine religious doctrines, yet fit none of the other Islamic sciences. Later scholars therefore mixed them with the questions of kalām to communicate realities and supply material that might help resolve difficulties. Otherwise there is no dispute that kalām proper extends only to the essence, attributes, prophecy, imamate, resurrection and the conditions of contingent beings connected with these.

Accordingly, in rejecting the view that kalām's subject matter is God's essence alone, or together with contingent essences under the aspect of dependence, scholars confined themselves to this objection: if that were so, establishing Him could not be one of kalām's sought conclusions. A science does not establish its own subject matter; this is done in a higher science, until one reaches a subject whose establishedness is evident, such as the existent. A science's reality consists in establishing a thing's essential attributes, which is what a compound existential judgement means. This plainly follows the simple existential judgement: one does not seek to establish something of what is not known to exist.

Yet there is no dispute that establishing the Necessary—meaning demonstrating His existence—is among kalām's highest aims. Whether He is the principle of contingent beings through choice or necessitation, immediately in all cases or through intermediaries in some, is another investigation. The claim that establishing Him belongs only to philosophical divine science and not to kalām is plainly false. Otherwise divine science would be one of the Islamic sciences—indeed their chief and head, the ground and foundation of the rules of revealed religion.

Some answer that the subject matter may be established within this science for two reasons. First, existence is one of its essential attributes because it is necessarily existent, unlike the subjects of other sciences, to which existence accrues through something distinct from them. This presumably is what is meant by the statement that a science does not establish its subject matter only where its investigation concerns conditions other than existence. Otherwise this distinction is supported neither by reason nor by transmission and scarcely has a meaning.

If it is said: “This works neither for someone who identifies existence with quiddity nor for someone who makes it additional and common, since an essential attribute must be proper to its subject,” we answer: whether His essence is existence itself or something other than it, either there is an acquired proposition whose predicate is ‘externally existent by necessity,’ in which case the reply succeeds, or there is not, in which case the original objection falls away.

Their second reason is that no religious science stands above kalām in which its subject matter could be established, so it must be established within kalām itself. This answer is open to criticism.

title: Five criticisms of that answer
en:
First, an essential attribute need not be uncaused by another. What is required is that its accrual to a thing not be mediated by its accruing to an external, noncoextensive thing. All agree that health and illness are essential attributes of a human being, motion and rest of body, and straightness and curvature of line, and so forth.

Second, their reasoning would imply that establishing the existence of any contingent thing could never be a question in any science. It would then be false that the existence of a science's subject matter is established in a higher science.

Third, once it has been assumed that a science establishes only its subject matter's essential attributes, the statement “a science does not establish its subject matter” would be redundant: what has existence as an essential attribute would be established in it, and what is not established would not be an essential attribute.

Fourth, the statement “every science has a subject matter, principles and questions” would no longer remain universal. Here “subject matter” means assent to its existence, the simple existential judgement, but in kalām that would have become one of the questions.

Fifth, sciences ascend according to the ascent of their subject matters. One science's being higher than another means only that its subject matter is more general. Kalām's subject matter should therefore be taken as the existent or the known. Otherwise philosophical divine science would stand above it in rank, even if kalām were nobler in another respect. You have already learned that the science establishing a religious science's subject matter or principles need not itself be religious; it is enough that it be certain and consistent with revelation.

title: Establishing a narrower subject in a broader science
en:
If it is said: “Your account now amounts to this: the existence proper to a discipline's subject matter is not established within it, even if existence is one of its essential attributes, because its investigation is confined to compound existential judgements. The subject's existence is assumed, being evident or established in a higher discipline. But then a difficulty arises: establishing it there is not a compound existential judgement, and the subject of this essential attribute is not something whose existence is already granted.”

We answer: the higher discipline has a more general subject matter. Its existence does not entail the existence of the narrower one. The narrower subject is therefore established within it by showing that the broader divides into this and something else, and that this division of it exists. This returns to a compound existential judgement concerning the broader subject. For example, divine science establishes that some existent is body, thereby establishing body's existence; natural philosophy establishes that some body is a sphere, thereby establishing the sphere's existence. title: Chapter two: knowledge and al-Rāzī's argument for its self-evidence
en:
**He says:** “Chapter two: knowledge.”

The Imām al-Rāzī held that the conception of knowledge is self-evident, for two reasons. First, knowledge is known, yet its conception cannot be acquired. That it is known is established by inward awareness. Acquisition is impossible because it would have to occur through something else already known: a thing cannot be acquired through itself or through something unknown. Yet that other thing is known only through knowledge. If knowledge were known through that other thing, circularity would follow. The route of immediate knowledge is therefore the only remaining possibility, as required.

Second, everyone's knowledge of his own existence is self-evident, meaning that it occurs without investigation or acquisition. This is a particular knowledge, preceded by knowledge without qualification, because it is composed of that and a particular determination. What precedes something self-evident is itself self-evident—indeed more deserving of being so. Knowledge without qualification is therefore self-evident, as required.

The reply to both arguments is that they fail to distinguish conceiving knowledge from possessing it. Regarding the first: if the conception of knowledge were acquired, it would depend upon conceiving something else. But conceiving that other thing does not depend upon conceiving knowledge, which would produce circularity. It depends upon possessing knowledge, on the ground that the qualified cannot occur without the unqualified. Indeed, if one rejects the universal's existence within particulars, it would not depend even upon possessing that [universal].

The *Mawāqif* says: “What we seek to know through something other than knowledge is the conception of the reality of knowledge.” This is imprecise in making the conception of the reality what one seeks to know. Better is the wording in the commentary on the *Mukhtaṣar*: “What is sought through another is the conception of the reality of knowledge.” Yet it too is imprecise when it says that conceiving something other than knowledge depends only upon possessing knowledge of it, namely a particular knowledge relating to that other thing: it makes no sense to say that something depends upon its own occurrence.

Regarding the second: what is self-evident for everyone is not the conception of his knowledge that he exists, but his possession of that knowledge. This does not require conceiving that knowledge, much less conceiving it self-evidently. Everyone likewise knows that he has a soul without knowing its reality.

title: Possessing a mental quality is not conceiving it
en:
If it is said: “Knowledge means only the soul's reaching a meaning and that meaning's occurrence in it. Knowledge is itself a mental meaning, so its occurrence in the soul is knowledge and conception of it. If possessing knowledge of one's existence is self-evident, conceiving that knowledge is self-evident, and consequently so is conceiving knowledge without qualification. Likewise, if conceiving the other thing through which the conception of knowledge is acquired depends upon possessing knowledge without qualification, it depends upon conceiving it: circularity follows.”

We answer: as already explained, mental meanings occur in the soul either in their own actuality—what is meant by actual, original existence—in which case this is being qualified by them, not conceiving them; or through their representations—what is meant by non-original existence, like a tree's shadow—in which case this is conceiving them, not being qualified by them. An unbeliever is qualified by unbelief through denial's occurring in his soul, even if he does not conceive it. He conceives faith through its concept's occurring in his soul without being qualified by faith.

The actual occurrence in the soul of knowledge of a thing is therefore not a conception of that knowledge. Conversely, the occurrence in the soul of the concept of knowing a thing is not being qualified by knowledge of that thing, though it may sometimes entail it. It is, however, being qualified by knowledge of the concept of knowledge, since that concept itself is present.

title: A strengthened version of al-Rāzī's argument
en:
If it is said: “The Imām's own formulation defeats that answer. He presents the first argument as follows. Acquiring knowledge depends upon possessing knowledge of another thing. This entails the possibility of knowing that one knows that other thing. If that possibility is actualised, knowledge of a particular knowledge would occur before knowledge of knowledge without qualification, which is impossible. Acquiring knowledge would thus entail conceiving another thing that entails the possibility of an impossibility, and would itself be impossible.

He anticipates this by explaining that this assent is self-evident in the sense that neither its judgement nor its terms require any investigation or acquisition, whether conceiving the terms is made a component or a condition of assent. It occurs even in those incapable of investigation and acquisition, such as the simple-minded and children.”

Moreover, if he means that knowing another thing entails the possibility of knowing that one knows it before acquiring the reality of knowledge, this is not conceded. If he means such possibility without qualification, it is unhelpful, since the possible act of knowing may occur only after that acquisition.

title: Defective definitions and al-Ghazālī's use of division and analogy
en:
**He says:** “Furthermore, most definitions of knowledge are defective…”

Examples are: recognising the known as it is; apprehending the known as it is; establishing the known as it is; believing a thing to be as it is; that through which a thing is known; and that which makes its bearer a knower. Their defects are evident. For the Imām, the Proof of Islam, however, these defects result from the obscurity of knowledge's meaning and the difficulty of defining it.

He says in the *Mustaṣfā*: “It may be difficult to define it really through a carefully formulated expression combining genus and differentia. This is difficult for most things, even for most sensible objects; how much more so for apprehensions! Its meaning is instead explained by division and analogy.”

Division distinguishes it from what may be confused with it, namely beliefs. It plainly differs from doubt and opinion through firmness, and from ignorance through correspondence [to what is the case]. Only the imitator's belief remains. Knowledge differs from that because a belief may persist while its object changes: someone may believe Zayd is in the house, then Zayd leaves while the belief remains. Knowledge, by contrast, changes when what is known changes and does not remain when the object's absence is believed. It is disclosure and an untying within belief, whereas belief is a knot upon the heart. Belief therefore disappears when someone raises doubts, unlike knowledge.

As for analogy, intellectual apprehension resembles visual apprehension. Vision means the impression of the visible thing's form—its corresponding likeness—upon the visual faculty, as a form is impressed in a mirror. Similarly, the intellect resembles a mirror in which the forms of intelligibles, their realities and quiddities as they are, are impressed. Knowledge is the intellect's taking the forms of intelligibles into itself, their impression upon it and their occurrence within it. Division thus separates knowledge from likely confusions, while this analogy enables you to understand its reality.

Such is his statement. It is clear that he means the difficulty of defining knowledge by a real definition, not the impossibility of an account that distinguishes it and conveys its reality. That claim is not implausible. Nor does he mean by “example” an instance of knowledge, such as our belief that one is half of two, as some have understood him.

The Imām al-Rāzī says that definitions of knowledge are defective because its quiddity is so manifest that nothing clearer can define it. Many investigators adopt this position. Some even say that disagreements about it arise from its extreme clarity, rather than its obscurity.

title: The several technical meanings of knowledge
en:
**He says:** “There is no dispute that its expression has several meanings…”

In technical usage “knowledge” has several meanings. One is intellectual apprehension, explained as the occurrence of a thing's form in the intellect. Its precise account and the answer to objections will come in the discussion of qualities. Some, observing that knowledge is an attribute of the knower while occurrence is an attribute of the form, substitute “the soul's reaching a meaning.” They draw upon what the Imām and others say: the first stage of the soul's reaching a meaning is awareness; its full grasp of the meaning is conception; its retaining the capacity to recover that meaning after its disappearance is preservation; seeking its recovery is recollection; and finding it again is remembrance. You know, however, that a form's occurrence in the intellect is also an attribute of the knower.

Another meaning is one kind of assent: that accompanied by firmness, correspondence and stability. This excludes opinion, compound ignorance and imitation, as will be explained.

A third meaning includes both corresponding conception and certain assent, in agreement with ordinary usage and language. Two formulations are given for it.

title: Knowledge as disclosure
en:
First: “An attribute through which what is referred to becomes manifest to its bearer.” That is, an attribute through which what is mentioned and attended to is completely disclosed to the bearer of that attribute, whether a human being or something else. “What is referred to” replaces “thing” so as to include both the existent and the nonexistent. One might suppose that it means “the known,” because mentioning knowledge implies mention of the known, and that the substitution is made to avoid circularity.

In any event, opinion and ignorance are excluded because neither contains disclosure. So too is the imitator's belief: it is a knot upon the heart, whereas disclosure is an opening and untying of that knot.

title: Knowledge as discrimination admitting no contradictory alternative
en:
Second: “An attribute yielding a discrimination among meanings that admits no contradictory alternative.” That is, an attribute followed, through God's creation, by a discrimination for its bearer among intelligible matters, whether universal or particular. Power and will are excluded, as is evident; so is sensory apprehension, whose discrimination concerns particular things. Anyone who makes knowledge include sensible objects omits this qualification.

The other apprehensions are excluded because admitting a contradictory alternative is evident in opinion, doubt and supposition of the less likely alternative, and even more evident in compound ignorance. The imitator's belief likewise admits it, because it may disappear when someone raises doubts; indeed, he may firmly adopt its contradictory. It is also said that compound ignorance is not discrimination, nor is a noncorresponding conception—for example, when a rational animal's form is impressed in the soul as its conception of a horse. A corresponding conception is included because it has no contradictory: forming a contradictory involves an element of judgement and composition. The difficulty in this is apparent.

Some restrict meanings to universals, favouring the convention of reserving *ʿilm* for universals and *maʿrifa* for particulars. The objection in the *Mawāqif* therefore does not apply: that this unnecessary addition makes the definition's extension questionable—that is, its application to all instances of the defined thing. This is like Ibn al-Ḥājib's statement that the active participle is an objection concerning the extension of the definition of noun, and the imperfect verb an objection concerning its exclusion of what does not belong. They say this is the grammarians' terminology.

The apparent meaning of “a discrimination admitting no contradictory alternative” concerns a contradictory of the discrimination itself. Since that makes little sense, some explain it as an attribute producing discrimination with a necessitation that admits no contrary. This is unsatisfactory. The correct account concerns the object of discrimination. As they say: believing a thing to be such-and-such, with no admissible alternative to its being so, is knowledge; believing it so while allowing a less likely alternative is opinion. The meaning is therefore an attribute yielding for the soul a discrimination of a meaning in such a way that no contradictory alternative is admitted concerning its object.

This is shown by their objection based on customary knowledge, such as knowing that a mountain is stone. It admits an alternative: it may cease to be stone and turn into gold, either because God creates gold in place of the stone, according to the investigators, or because He removes from the stone's parts the attribute making them stone and creates in them the attribute making them gold, according to some theologians who hold that the substances in all bodies are homogeneous.

title: Epistemic certainty and metaphysical possibility
en:
The answer is that “admitting no contradictory alternative” in knowledge means that the knower allows none, either actually or by implication. With conception, this is because it has no contradictory, or because admitting a contradictory makes no sense without an element of judgement. With assent, this is because the firmness of the judgement rests upon a sufficient ground and so admits no disappearance [while that ground obtains]. Customary cognitions are of this kind: their firmness rests upon a ground, namely custom. They admit a contradictory only in the sense that supposing it to occur entails no intrinsic impossibility, because they concern things intrinsically possible, which may occur or fail to occur. We likewise judge with certainty that a body we see is white, although in itself it may be white or not.

In sum, admitting a contradictory alternative means that the person judging allows it actually and at present, as in opinion, whose object is not firmly affirmed; or by implication and prospectively, as in the imitator's belief. The latter's firmness rests upon no adequate sensory, rational or customary ground, so it may disappear; indeed, firm belief in the contrary may arise. This also answers the objection to certain accounts of knowledge from the imitator's belief, especially a corresponding one: although it admits no contrary either in reality or in the believer's present judgement, the relevant issue is not bare rational possibility, as the customary examples show.

title: Conception and assent: the structure of the division
en:
**He says:** “The second investigation.”

**I say:** The division of cognition into conception and assent is well known. Some find it difficult because the two entail one another: no assent occurs without conception; indeed, they say that a real conception does not occur without assent establishing [the reality], and that only nominal conception is at issue. They therefore divide cognition into bare conception, conditioned by the absence of judgement, and assent.

Others answer that entailment in existence does not conflict with opposition in application, as with even and odd. Dividing cognition into conception conditioned by the absence of judgement and assent is not exhaustive, because the conceptions of assent's two terms would fall outside it. In general, the scholars explicitly say that the conception included in assent is precisely the conception contrasted with assent: conception without judgement being made a condition, meaning that judgement is not included in its account—not conception conditioned by judgement's absence. The Imām and al-Kātibī expressly identify this as the meaning of “bare conception” and “conception alone.”

The division amounts to this: either judgement is included in the cognition, making it assent, or it is not, making it conception. On the Imām's explicit account, assent means judgement together with the conceptions connected with it, not apprehension qualified by judgement, as his phrases “apprehension accompanied by judgement” and “apprehension to which judgement is attached” might initially suggest. How could the latter be his intention, when he introduces these statements to argue that conception is a part of assent? Yet he also frequently identifies assent with judgement itself, and describes judgement sometimes as an act, sometimes as a quiddity called inner speech belonging neither to belief nor to will.

The majority hold that assent is judgement itself, a kind of cognition differing in reality from conception. It concerns only the relation, whereas conception concerns both the relation and other things. When you doubt whether the world is temporally originated, you have conceived the world, the temporally originated and the relation between them, without judgement or assent. Once the demonstration is supplied, you cognise the relation through another kind of cognition called judgement and assent. Its reality is the soul's submission to and acceptance of the relation's obtaining or not obtaining. In Persian it is expressed by *girawīdan*, as Ibn Sīnā explicitly says.

title: Ibn Sīnā on conceiving a proposition and assenting to it
en:
This is what the *Shifāʾ* says: in your statement “whiteness is an accident,” conception is the occurrence in the mind of the form of this combination and of what composes it, such as whiteness and accident. Assent is the occurrence in the mind of this form's relation to the things themselves as corresponding to them. Denial is the opposite.

This statement indicates that truth is what a declarative utterance or proposition signifies; falsity is only a rational possibility. title: Immediate and inferential cognition
en:
His words “necessary awareness judges…” mean that conception and assent are each divided into inferential and immediate. We find within ourselves that some conceptions and assents require investigation—for example, conceiving angels and jinn and assenting to the world's temporal origination—while others do not, such as conceiving existence and nonexistence and assenting to the impossibility of contradictories occurring together.

The requirement or independence is intrinsic. Thus a judgement intrinsically independent of investigation is immediate, even if its two terms are acquired, in accordance with the majority's account: immediate assent is what requires no investigation or acquisition once its terms have been conceived. The *Mawāqif*'s wording—“some is immediate by inward awareness and some inferential by necessity”—may suggest that the second is not established by inward awareness, but the intention is what we have explained.

The judge Abū Bakr defined immediate knowledge as what binds the created soul so that it finds no way to free itself from it. He specified the created soul because immediate and inferential are divisions of originated knowledge. It is objected that the soul may be separated from immediate knowledge: it may disappear after occurring because sleep, inattention or another contrary intervenes; or it may never occur because a condition is absent, such as attention, conception of the terms, the soul's readiness, sensation or experience—conditions upon which some immediate cognitions depend.

The reply is that the soul lacks the power to free itself from it. In the cases mentioned, separation does not occur through the creature's power. This is what the *Mawāqif* means by saying that his wording suggests ability: when we say someone finds or does not find a way to do something, we mean that he can or cannot do it.

In sum, applying “necessary” to knowledge derives from necessity in the sense of lacking the power to act or refrain, as in the movement of someone trembling. It is therefore sometimes defined as knowledge whose acquisition lies outside a creature's power. But actual occurrence is intended here, as is indicated by making necessary knowledge a division of originated knowledge and as the judge's wording expressly states. This excludes knowledge of such matters as the full detail of numbers and figures, which the servant can neither acquire nor free himself from [because he does not possess it].

If it is said that both formulations also include knowledge resulting from investigation, since once it occurs one can neither acquire it again nor free oneself from it, the answer is that immediate knowledge involves continuous absence of control. With inferential knowledge, control disappears only after acquisition. Beforehand one can obtain it by acquiring it or avoid it by not acquiring it.

If it is said: “Even granting that the judge means inability to free oneself, separation, whether voluntary or not, contradicts binding necessity,” we answer that “binding” means established occurrence, or inability to separate by one's power, the latter part of the statement explaining the former.

title: Inferential, acquired and inspired knowledge
en:
He defined inferential knowledge as what sound investigation includes: what does not fail to accompany it in the customary course when its conditions are met. He did not say “what investigation necessitates,” because, as will be explained, the conclusion does not follow investigation by necessitation. Nor did he say “what occurs after sound investigation,” since immediate cognitions may also occur then, such as awareness of pleasure or pain arising at that time. “What sound investigation yields,” with customary succession intended, would have been clearer.

“Acquired” is opposed to “immediate” and is synonymous with “inferential” for someone who recognises investigation as the sole route of acquisition. For someone who allows acquisition through purification or inspiration without treating these as involving investigation, acquired knowledge is broader than inferential knowledge. Nor do the two invariably accompany one another in customary experience, despite what is said in the *Mawāqif*, unless purification, inspiration and the like are treated as extraordinary occurrences.

“Acquired” is also used for what results from voluntarily undertaking its causes, such as directing the intellect or a sense toward something, and “immediate” for its opposite. Acquired knowledge that is inferential is then specially called demonstrative or inferentially established knowledge.

title: Al-Rāzī's denial that conceptions can be acquired
en:
**He says:** “The Imām chose…”

**I say:** The Imām al-Rāzī chose the view that every conception that occurs is immediate. Acquisition is impossible both on the side of what is acquired—the object sought—and on the side of what acquires it—the means of acquisition.

On the first side, the object sought is either known, in which case seeking and acquiring it is impossible because this would obtain what is already obtained; or unknown, in which case directing oneself toward it is impossible. Two objections are raised. First, why may it not be known in one respect, allowing attention to it, and unknown in another, allowing inquiry? Second, the argument also applies to acquiring assent, although assent is acquired.

He answers the first: either it is sought under its known aspect, which is impossible because it is already obtained, or under its unknown aspect, which is impossible because attention cannot be directed toward it. He answers the second: assent's object—the proposition or relation—is known conceptually, so attention to it is possible, but unknown with respect to assent, so seeking that assent is possible. Conception is different: what is unknown conceptually is wholly unknown, since no cognition precedes conception. In short, assent's object can be the object of another cognition before assent, namely conception; conception's object cannot.

The reply is that we choose the case in which it is known in one respect. We do not concede that attention to its unknown aspect is then impossible. That would be so only if the known aspect were not one of its own aspects or considerations, taking it out of complete unknownness. For example, we know that we possess something through which life and apprehensions occur, and then seek to know it in its reality or through attributes distinguishing it from everything else, as a definition or description provides. What is sought and unknown is therefore not confined to either the reality or an accidental attribute.

The *Mawāqif*'s statement that the essence is unknown and some considerations are known establishes the more important point—the possibility of acquiring a real conception—and draws attention to the fact that what one seeks to conceive must be unknown in its essence. If a thing is already known in its reality and one seeks to establish an accidental attribute of it, this is done through a proof, not a definition. If one seeks to conceive the attribute itself, it is that attribute which is unknown in its reality.

The *Talkhīṣ al-Muḥaṣṣal* says that the known and unknown aspects both belong to a third thing, which is the object sought. This binds the Imām by his own admission that what is known generally is known in one respect and unknown in another. The respects differ: one is known without generality or indistinctness, and the other is entirely unknown; their conjunction in one thing merely makes one suppose that there is general knowledge. Otherwise, the same author explicitly says in the critique of the *Tanzīl al-afkār* that the unknown object sought is the reality of the quiddity known through some of its accidental attributes.
