title: The argument from the means of acquiring a conception
en:
As for the second side, the acquiring means—that which defines a quiddity—cannot be the quiddity itself, since nothing is clearer or known earlier than itself. It must therefore be all its parts, which are the quiddity itself, restoring the difficulty; some of its parts; or something external to it. The last category includes a combination of internal and external elements. Anyone who lists that combination separately means by “internal” and “external” what is purely internal or purely external.

Some of the parts can define the quiddity only by making one of its parts known. If all the parts were already known, or remained unknown, the supposed definition would not define: it would not cause knowledge of the quiddity or lead to its conception. If the part making another known is that same part, the difficulty returns. If it is another part, definition through something external follows, since every part is external to another. Even if parts are assumed to include one another, the argument shifts to defining the part composed of this part and another, restoring either the original difficulty or definition through something external.

Definition through something external is also impossible. An external feature provides knowledge of a quiddity only if one knows that it belongs exclusively to it: that it is established for it and absent from everything else. This is an assent requiring conception of the quiddity, producing circularity, and detailed conception of everything else, which is unlimited and therefore impossible.

There is an imprecision in the *Mawāqif*: “If the part defines the quiddity, it defines itself—which has been refuted—and what is external—which we shall refute.” What will be refuted is definition **through** something external, not definition **of** something external. Perhaps the preposition is omitted, meaning “defines through what is external”; or the intention is that it defines something external to the other parts, so the defining part is external to what it defines. The consequence is definition through an external feature, not merely defining something external.

The argument in the *Muḥaṣṣal* alleges both impossibilities because it assumes that defining a quiddity defines each of its parts. Since this is readily denied, we have confined ourselves to one of them, following the formulation in the *Maṭālib al-ʿāliya*. It is evident that challenging any premise suffices to defeat the argument. But since scholars allow definition through all the parts, some parts and external features, we must answer all three difficulties.

title: Knowing the parts and knowing their whole
en:
The first is answered as follows. Although all the parts are intrinsically the quiddity itself, defining it through them would be impossible only if they did not differ from it in consideration. The precise point is that several conceptions may concern the parts, which are considered one by one, distinctly and in order. They then constitute the acquiring means, the definition. Or one conception may concern them, considering the aggregate as an aggregate. They then constitute what is acquired, the thing defined. This is what is meant by saying that the defined thing is grasped collectively and the definition distinctly. There is no impossibility in the conception of the whole following from, and being caused by, the collection of conceptions.

If it is said: “If the collection of conceptions yields the conception of the whole, either the former are present, in which case the latter is already present and investigation acquires nothing; or they are absent, in which case they cannot define but must themselves be sought. The argument then transfers to what produces them. The same applies to defining through some parts, through an external feature, and indeed to acquiring assents.”

We answer: the parts may be known but dispersed among other cognitions. Investigation is required to bring them together in an ordered presence that yields the conception of the quiddity. This is acquisition. In sum, it comes back to acquiring the formal component. Apply the same reasoning to the other cases.

title: Criticism of al-Ījī's objection to conception of a whole
en:
The *Mawāqif* objects to the claim that a collection of conceptions produces the conception of the whole: “The truth is that when the parts are brought to mind in order and thus become present, they are the quiddity itself. There is not a present aggregate producing some other thing called the quiddity. Similarly, when external parts are present, they are the external composite itself, not something upon which the composite follows.”

Taken as it stands, this is no objection. The claim is not that the aggregate of parts produces another thing that is the quiddity, but that the conceptions of the parts may produce another thing, namely the conception of the whole, the conception of the quiddity. If he intends to deny that, his denial is false, supported neither by immediate awareness nor by demonstration, and contradicted by inward experience. The analogy with external existence has no force: the intellect's modes of consideration are unrestricted. It can consider one existent now as a whole, now part by part.

His proposed solution adds only: “The definition is the collection of things each of which is prior.” This is unhelpful, since the defined thing is likewise such a collection. To explain difference and causation, one must therefore say that those things, distinctly considered, are the definition, and collectively considered, the defined thing. That is precisely what the scholars mean.

title: Definition through some parts or an external feature
en:
Regarding the second difficulty, we deny that what defines a quiddity must make one of its parts known. The parts may already be known but require presentation together, in order and distinguished from other things; the definition provides this. Although the quiddity is intrinsically the parts themselves, knowing it need not be knowing the parts in the sense of having several conceptions of them. They must be considered together and distinguished from other things.

Alternatively, the parts may remain unknown while the definition supplies a conception of the quiddity under an aspect distinguishing it from everything else, without comprehending the reality of any part. Even if the premise is granted, the defining part may be intrinsically the same as the defined part, differing through collective and distinct consideration, as in defining a quiddity through its parts. Or it may be another part, and definition through an external feature is valid, as will be explained.

This answers the objections: “All the parts are the quiddity itself, so how could knowing it fail to be knowing them?” “A definition causes knowledge of the thing—its occurrence in the mind—so how could it fail to produce any of its parts?” And: “If the cause of a thing's occurrence were not the cause of any part, every part could occur without it, and therefore the whole could occur without it; it would not be a cause.” Consider the arrangement joining the parts: it causes the composite's occurrence without causing any individual part to occur.

Regarding the third difficulty, we deny that definition through an external feature depends upon knowing its exclusivity. It depends upon the exclusivity itself. The mind passes from conceiving what entails something to conceiving its mental concomitant, even without prior knowledge of that entailment. Even if the premise is granted, conceiving the thing under some aspect and everything else generally is sufficient. A body's exclusive occupancy of this region is analogous, although it rests on the impossibility of one body occupying two regions or two spatial occupants occupying one region.

It is with this concession in view that some say: an attribute suitable for defining something must be a concomitant evidently established for all its instances and evidently absent from everything else. Note that although it must be a concomitant in predication, it must be an antecedent of entailment in conception [so that conceiving it leads to conceiving the defined thing].

title: Are all the parts identical with the composite?
en:
One investigator answers the first difficulty by denying that all a quiddity's parts are the quiddity itself. Indeed, he declares this false, arguing that things each prior to something cannot be identical with that posterior thing. He then says that, when combined, they may become the posterior quiddity and produce knowledge of it: knowing the genus, differentia and qualifying combination precedes knowing the genus qualified by the differentia; these are its parts and through them it becomes known.

This denial is rejected sometimes by an appeal to immediate awareness, sometimes by argument. If all a thing's parts are not the thing itself, either they are external to it, which is plainly false, or internal, in which case it is composed of them and something else. They would then be only some of its parts, not all. Again, if a thing differs from all its parts, its complete reality is either that different thing alone—in which case the supposed parts are not its parts—or that together with the parts, in which case the specified parts are not all its parts.

The argument from priority is weak. Each part's priority to a thing does not entail the whole's priority to it, which would prevent its being the posterior thing itself. If it did, the whole would be prior to itself, since each part is necessarily prior to it.

His wording suggests that by “all the parts” he means everything internal to a thing without considering composition and conjunction; by “the composite” he means those things together with their conjunction. Al-Kashshī similarly says that the bare totality of a thing's parts is not the thing itself: it is those parts together with a specific unified arrangement through which it is what it is.

But this returns to the view that a complete definition defines through all the material parts, whose presence in the mind produces a form corresponding to what exists concretely. This investigator himself rejected that view: a complete definition includes not only its material parts, genus and differentia, but also its formal part, their order, because genus and differentia without order do not constitute a complete definition. He nevertheless insists that all the material and formal parts are not the composite itself, since they are causes and it is their effect. It is self-evident, he says, that someone producing two by producing one, producing another one, and joining them, does not produce two through two itself, but through all its material and formal parts.

**I say:** Since inferential cognitions terminate in immediate ones, scholars made establishing immediate cognition and answering its deniers part of kalām's principles. This enables one to determine whether what is presented as the endpoint of a syllogism's premises and claimed to be immediate really belongs to that class.

They did not attempt an exhaustive classification of immediate conceptions; these apparently return to self-evident and observed cognitions. They classified immediate assents into six: self-evident, observed, those whose syllogisms accompany them, experiential, multiply transmitted, and intuitive.

The reason is this. Either conceiving a proposition's terms, once the conditions of apprehension such as attention and sound faculties are present, suffices for the intellect's judgement, or it does not. In the first case it is self-evident. In the second, something must be added to assist the intellect, to supplement the proposition, or both. The first yields observed propositions, which require sensation. In the second, the added item either invariably accompanies the terms, yielding propositions whose syllogisms accompany them, or does not. If it does not, but is obtained readily, the propositions are intuitive; otherwise they are inferential rather than immediate. In the third case, if the assistance comes through reports the propositions are multiply transmitted; otherwise they are experiential.

title: Self-evident, observed and readily mediated propositions
en:
Self-evident propositions, also called primary propositions, are those the intellect judges merely by conceiving their two terms: one is half of two; one body cannot occupy two places at one time. The intellect may withhold judgement because the terms have not been conceived, as in “things equal to one thing are equal”; because natural intellectual capacity is deficient, as in children and the simple-minded; because the original disposition has been corrupted by contrary beliefs, as among some ignorant people; or because God does not create the judgement, according to our doctrine.

Observed propositions are those the intellect judges through the external senses, in which case they are called sensory—for example, that the sun shines and fire is hot—or the internal senses, in which case they are called inwardly experienced—for example, that we have fear and anger. They include what we find through our souls without bodily instruments, such as awareness of ourselves and our states. All sensory judgements are particular: sensation tells us only that this fire is hot. “Every fire is hot” is an intellectual judgement obtained with the aid of sensation of particular instances and recognition of its causes.

The propositions called *fiṭriyyāt* are those the intellect judges through a middle term that does not escape it when the two terms are conceived. This is what was meant by something inseparably accompanying the proposition. They are therefore called “propositions whose syllogisms accompany them”: for example, that four is even because it divides into two equal parts.

title: Experience, multiple transmission and intuition
en:
Experiential propositions are those the intellect judges when repeated observation assists it and a concealed syllogism yielding certainty accompanies the proposition. That syllogism is: recurrence in one regular manner must have a cause, even if its nature is unknown; whenever the cause's presence is known, the effect's presence is therefore known with certainty. An example is the judgement that scammony purges yellow bile.

Multiply transmitted propositions are those the intellect judges through numerous informants' testimony concerning a possible matter grounded in observation, their number being such that collusion in falsehood is impossible. Hearing their reports assists the intellect, while a concealed syllogism supplements the proposition: if this judgement were not true, this multitude would not have reported it.

Intuitive propositions are those the intellect judges through a powerful intuition of the soul, removing doubt and producing certainty upon observing indications. An example is that the moon receives its light from the sun, inferred from the changing configurations of its illumination as its positions relative to the sun change. Its sunward side is always illuminated, and its light shifts toward opposition to the sun. The intellect intuits that this would not occur unless its light came from the sun.

These resemble experiential propositions in repeated observation and the accompanying concealed syllogism. In experiential propositions, however, the cause is known to be a cause but its nature is unknown; in intuitive propositions it is known in both respects. Its recognition occurs through intuition rather than discursive thought; otherwise the cognition would be acquired. You will learn the meaning of intuition in the discussion of the soul.

title: Are all six classes really immediate?
en:
**He says:** “They may be restricted to self-evident and observed cognitions.”

The *Muḥaṣṣal* states that immediate cognitions are inwardly experienced cognitions—which have little use in sciences because they are not shared—sensory cognitions and self-evident cognitions. The author of the *Mawāqif* follows him, although elsewhere he identifies immediate cognitions as the six already mentioned, together with estimative judgements concerning sensible things, such as the judgement that every body lies in a direction.

He offers two explanations of the *Muḥaṣṣal*. First, self-evident propositions include *fiṭriyyāt*: since the middle term inseparably accompanies the conception of the two terms, it is as though the intellect requires only those conceptions. Sensory propositions include experiential and multiply transmitted propositions, since the intellect's judgement in these rests upon sensation, though with repetition; the same applies to intuitive propositions.

Second, whether experiential, multiply transmitted and intuitive propositions are immediate is debatable, as the Imām explains in the *Mulakhkhaṣ*, because each involves consideration of a concealed syllogism. The same applies to propositions whose syllogisms accompany them. Some dispute whether experiential and intuitive propositions are even certain, let alone immediate; many scholars classify intuitive propositions among opinions.

Investigators who deny that these four classes are immediate nevertheless deny that they are inferential: they occupy an intermediate position because they require no discursive acquisition. The Imām, the Proof of Islam, suggests this when he says that knowledge from multiple transmission is immediate in the sense that it requires no awareness of an intervening means leading to it, even though that means is present in the mind. It is not immediate in the sense of arising without an intermediary, as in “the existent is not nonexistent.” Two premises must be present: this multitude, despite its number and diversity, has no common ground for agreeing to lie; and they have agreed in reporting the event. But one need not arrange these premises or be aware of their mediation and production of the conclusion.

This shows that the dispute is verbal, resting upon whether “immediate” means requiring no intermediary at all or what we find ourselves compelled to accept.

title: Hearing a report, establishing its attribution and accepting its content
en:
If it is said: “Multiply transmitted reports belong to what is perceived by hearing. They should therefore be immediate without dispute, like knowing that fire is hot.”

We answer: the issue is knowledge of the content of the report heard through multiple transmission—the existence of Mecca, for example. That is intellectually known, with repeated hearing as its instrument. If what is multiply transmitted reports the attribution of another report to a truthful speaker, knowledge of the latter report's content is acquired by agreement.

For example, suppose it is multiply transmitted that the Prophet said: “Proof is incumbent upon the claimant, and the oath upon the one who denies.” Knowing that this is the informants' sound is immediate sensory knowledge. Knowing that the reported statement is the Prophet's speech is what is obtained from the multiply transmitted proposition whose immediacy is disputed. Knowing that proof is obligatory upon the claimant is acquired by arranging two premises: this is the Prophet's report; and whatever the Prophet reports has true content, because his truthfulness has been established through the indication of miracles.

Saying that a hadith is multiply transmitted therefore means that the report attributing it to the Prophet is multiply transmitted, whether that hadith is itself a declarative report or a performative utterance.

title: Those who deny the foundations of knowledge
en:
**He says:** “As for the deniers…”

The people of truth agree that sensory and self-evident cognitions are first principles for arguments binding upon others. Some people deny this: some challenge sensory cognitions and restrict first principles to self-evident ones; some do the reverse; and some challenge both. Each group has specious arguments. The Imām discusses these at length, multiplying examples, and attributes to the leading philosophers the view that sensory cognitions are not certain.

It is objected that most of the philosophers' certain cognitions rest upon sensory cognition, and their immediate first principles draw upon it. They expressly state that experiential, multiply transmitted and intuitive cognitions begin from sensation of particulars, and that children acquire primary cognitions through an intellectual readiness produced by sensing particulars. How could denial of sensory certainty be attributed to them?

The defence is that the intellect's firm judgements drawn from sensation may depend upon conditions whose nature, time of occurrence and manner of occurrence are not known. Accordingly, the philosophers established optics to explain where error arises concerning sensible things and which judgements are certain; similarly they established the discipline of sophistical reasoning to explain this concerning intelligibles.

The *Talkhīṣ al-Muḥaṣṣal* says that sense does not judge, since combining terms in a judgement is not its function: its function is apprehension alone, and judgement belongs to intellect. This is not merely a verbal objection to whether sense or intellect through sense is the judge. It serves the further point: a sensible object, insofar as it is sensed, is not characterised as certain or uncertain; it receives that characterisation only together with an intellectual judgement. The disputed thesis would therefore mean that intellectual judgements about sensible things are uncertain because they sometimes err. But error also occurs with purely intelligible things, and the thesis cannot properly be attributed to the philosophers, who explicitly affirm the contrary.

When the Imām argues that the cited doubts establish that sense can err and therefore needs a higher judge distinguishing its correct from incorrect judgements, so that sense cannot be the first judge, the reply is that sense is never the judge: intellect judges in every case.

As for explaining the causes of error in the Imām's examples, the author acknowledges that this merely alerts someone who trusts, or professes trust in, primary and sensory cognitions to ways of escaping the difficulties at the sites of error. Determining what is correct and mistaken is then referred to clear intellect, without needing a proof establishing confidence in sensation, an answer to every doubt, or an exhaustive examination of causes and their absence.

title: Sensory error does not abolish sensory certainty
en:
The doubts amount to this: sensory judgement is untrustworthy. Concerning universals, sense does not encompass them—how could it, when they are not confined to actual individuals? Concerning particulars, it often errs by judging sensible things otherwise than they are. We see the small as large and the large as small, one as many and many as one, the stationary as moving, and so forth. A grape in water appears like a pear, a distant jar like a small jug, and the moon in water like two moons. Differently coloured lines extending from a millstone's centre to its circumference appear, when it rotates, as one colour blended from them all. A person on a ship sees the ship as stationary although it moves and the shore as moving although it is stationary, and there are other examples.

The answer is that error in some cases does not conflict with firm, corresponding judgement in many others, such as that the sun shines and fire is hot. Intellect is certain that no error occurs there without needing investigation, even if assisted by conditions not known in detail.

This is what the *Mawāqif* says: the doubts imply that intellect should not judge sensory matters firmly merely from sensation; they do not imply that its firm judgement, where it does judge firmly, is untrustworthy, or that every such judgement remains open to uncertainty. In the phrase “and its being open to uncertainty,” the expression is therefore nominative and coordinated with “that its judgement be distrusted,” not genitive and coordinated with “its firm judgement,” as might be supposed; the latter construction has little sense.

title: Objections to self-evident principles
en:
**He says:** “Some challenge self-evident cognitions.”

They say that these derive from sensory cognitions, since human beings recognise them only after sensing particulars and noticing their agreements and differences. Criticising a derivative does not necessarily undermine its source; that would follow only if the derivative intrinsically followed from it.

Their objection is that the clearest and highest self-evident assent—negation and affirmation neither coexist nor are both absent, meaning that a thing either is or is not—is itself untrustworthy. That it is clearest is evident. It is highest, meaning prior, because all other principles depend upon it. For instance, in “the whole is greater than the part,” one observes that otherwise the remaining part would both be and not be. In “one body cannot occupy two places at one time,” if it occupied both, one would be two, so one of the two similar things would both be and not be. Other cases follow this pattern.

It is untrustworthy, they say, because knowing this proposition's reality and certainty depends upon conceiving existence and nonexistence—being and not-being—determining what subjecthood and predication mean, and answering doubts about these matters. These three matters are established only through subtle investigations. If those investigations succeed, they necessarily depend upon the truth of this proposition as the first of first principles. Circularity follows, and something would be inferential on the very supposition that it is immediate, which is impossible. If anything remains obscure, firm assent to the proposition is not obtained, which is the desired conclusion.

The answer is that immediate intellect is certain of this proposition and its truth without investigation or inference, either to establish the relation or to dispel objections. The doubts raised do not undermine that certainty, and they cannot be refuted for someone who acknowledges no self-evident principles. We may turn away from him or draw his attention to them, hoping that he acknowledges them or becomes ready for investigation and qualified for discussion.

title: Conceiving nonexistence without making it externally existent
en:
One doubt is that this assent depends upon conceiving existence, nonexistence and other things. Conception requires establishedness, at least in the mind; but the establishedness of absolute nonexistence is contradictory. Furthermore, absolute nonexistence must be capable of being negated if any existence is to be established. This negation would then be both a subdivision of absolute nonexistence, because it is a relative nonexistence, and a coordinate alternative to it, because it removes and negates it.

The answer is that a meaning may be unestablished in its own nature and concept yet established through occurring in the intellect. Nor is it impossible for it to be a subdivision of nonexistence insofar as it is a relative nonexistence and a coordinate alternative to it in its concept. This will be explained more fully in the discussion of nonexistence.

title: Predication, existence and the alleged union of two things
en:
Another doubt: if existence is taken as a predicate in this disjunction—“body either exists or does not exist”—then either a thing's existence is its quiddity, making the affirmative part redundant although it is certainly informative, and the negative part contradictory, since unrestricted negation contradicts permanent affirmation; or existence differs from quiddity. In the latter case, affirmation makes existence inhere in something nonexistent if the subject is taken without existence, or produces an infinite regress of existences if it is taken as existent. This will be explained and answered in the discussion of existence.

Furthermore, [the objection continues,] predication makes a thing something other than itself, uniting two things. Negation involves conceiving negation, which entails its establishedness, and a quiddity's being without existence, which entails existence's inhering in a nonexistent when existence is established for it.

The answer is that two things may differ in one respect and be one in another. Subject and predicate differ conceptually but are identical in what they identify. What is called “body” is the very same thing called “existent.” Nor is it impossible for absolute negation to be established through occurring in the intellect, or for existence to belong to what was not [already independently] existent, as will be explained, God willing.

title: Relations, qualification and mental judgements
en:
All this concerns existence taken as a predicate. If it is taken as a copula—“body either is black or is not black”—the affirmative part again supposedly unites two things, which has already been answered. Moreover, since the predicate is an attribute, the subject possesses being-qualified-by-it. This is positive because its contradictory, not-being-qualified, is negative. The body must be qualified by this qualification, producing an infinite regress of qualifications.

Calling these intellectual considerations does not, according to the objection, resolve the difficulty: qualification is a relation and must inhere in the related things, not the intellect. Moreover, if intellectual judgement does not correspond to external reality, it is ignorance. If affirmation is thus refuted, only the negative part would always be true, whereas you allow affirmation sometimes to be true.

The answer, to be explained later, is that a negative linguistic form, such as “not-being-qualified,” need not signify a negative reality. Even if it does, the contradictory of a negative need not be positive. Moreover, the truth of mental judgements is not determined by correspondence to what exists externally. Relations and correlations occurring only in the intellect may still be attributed to external things: those things are such that, when someone apprehends them, those relations arise in his intellect.

Another doubt is: “We do not concede that nothing intervenes between existence and nonexistence.” Its answer will follow; in any case, no intermediate can be conceived between being and not-being. The *Mawāqif* says that the advocates of an intermediate are sufficiently numerous for their testimony to constitute proof. This means that it could constitute proof when reporting something sensible; in an intelligible matter it at least gives rise to a doubt.

Even if it does, the contradictory of a negative need not be positive. Moreover, the truth of mental judgements is not determined by correspondence to what exists externally. Relations and correlations occurring only in the intellect may still be attributed to external things: those things are such that, when someone apprehends them, those relations arise in his intellect.

Another doubt is: “We do not concede that nothing intervenes between existence and nonexistence.” Its answer will follow; in any case, no intermediate can be conceived between being and not-being. The Mawāqif says that the advocates of an intermediate are sufficiently numerous for their testimony to constitute proof. This means that it could constitute proof when reporting something sensible; in an intelligible matter it at least gives rise to a doubt.

title: Sophistical positions and the limits of disputation
en:
**He says:** “Some challenge both.”

That is, both sensory and self-evident cognitions. These are the sophists. The *Talkhīṣ al-Muḥaṣṣal* says that some people imagine sophists to be a group with a creed and doctrine, divided into three classes. The agnostics say: “We doubt, and we doubt that we doubt,” and so on. The obstinate say that every proposition, self-evident or inferential, has an equally acceptable opposing proposition. The relativists say that every group's doctrine is true relative to that group and false relative to its opponents; both contradictories may be true relative to two different people, while nothing is true in reality itself.

According to the investigators, sophistry derives from *sūfā asṭā*, meaning the science of error and counterfeit wisdom: *sūfā* names knowledge and *asṭā* error. No group in the world could actually adhere to such a doctrine; rather, everyone who errs is a sophist precisely where he errs.

The contradiction in the obstinate and relativist positions is apparent, since they acknowledge the truth of an affirmation or negation, especially when they defend their claim through an argument. The agnostics, by contrast, persist in uncertainty about everything to which they attend, even whether they are doubting. They argue that neither sense nor intellect is trustworthy, on the basis of the preceding groups' doubts; inference is derivative from both and cannot be trusted either. Only suspension remains. Their purpose in this argument is to produce doubt and suspicion, not establish or deny anything. Their position is therefore sounder in method than that of the obstinate and relativists.

The investigators maintain that inquiry and disputation with them are impossible. Disputation imparts the unknown through the known, but they acknowledge nothing known and insist upon denying even immediate sensory and self-evident cognitions. Undertaking to prove these would accept their position and fulfil their aim: that sensory and self-evident cognitions are not immediately given but require acquisition. On our account, something immediate cannot be unknown and then obtained through something known.

The way to deal with them, [the author says,] is therefore to inflict pain, even with fire. Either they acknowledge pain, which is sensory, and its difference from pleasure, which is intellectual, thereby invalidating their position and extinguishing their creed; or they persist in denial and burn, thereby ending the disturbance they provoke and extinguishing the fire they kindle.

title: Chapter three: rational investigation
en:
**He says:** “Chapter three: rational investigation.”

He includes six investigations, the first explaining its reality. Plainly, not every object sought can be obtained from any starting point whatsoever; appropriate principles are required. Nor do those principles lead to it in any arrangement whatsoever; a specific configuration is required.

When we seek to acquire a conception or assent, the object must already be apprehended under some aspect. Starting from it, the soul moves among the forms stored within it, passing from one to another until it finds the object's principles—essential constituents, accidental attributes or middle terms—and brings them distinctly and determinately to mind. It then moves among them, arranging them in a particular order that yields either conception of the object in its reality or under an aspect distinguishing it from everything else, or assent to it, certain or otherwise.

There are thus two movements: the first obtains the matter, the second the form. The principles, insofar as they are reached, terminate the first movement; insofar as one returns from them, they initiate the second; insofar as they are worked upon to produce the specific arrangement, they are the matter of the second. Rational investigation in its full reality comprises both movements. They belong to motion in quality, through forms and qualities successively occurring in the soul.

There must also be orientation toward the object, removal of obstructing inattention and incompatible forms, consideration of intelligibles so that some are selected and others discarded, arrangement of what is selected, and an intended end.

title: Alternative definitions of investigation
en:
Explanations of investigation often mention only some of its parts or concomitants, either because these suffice to distinguish it or through a technical convention. It is thus called the mind's movement toward the principles of the object sought; its movement from principles to sought conclusions; or the arrangement of known things to reach the unknown. Here “known” means present to the intellect, including opinion and compound ignorance.

Definition through the differentia alone or the distinctive property alone is included because these employ a derived expression, such as “rational” or “capable of laughter,” which contains an element of composition and order between the qualified thing and its attribute. Alternatively, the definition is restricted to investigation involving composition and arrangement, since definition through a single expression is rare and its exclusion is harmless. This is what Ibn Sīnā means by calling definition through a single expression deficient.

The Imām substitutes “assents” for “known things,” in accordance with his view that conceptions cannot be acquired. He also frequently identifies investigation with the ordered cognitions themselves.

Someone who defines it as arranging known or believed matters to reach an unknown means by “known” conception and firm, corresponding, stable assent—that is, certainty—and by “believed” what contrasts with certainty, including mere opinion, compound ignorance and belief, as explicitly stated in the commentary on the *Ishārāt*.

Consequently, the following objection in the *Mawāqif* does not apply: “This cannot define sound investigation; otherwise belief would need qualification by correspondence to exclude corruption through false believed matter, and ‘to reach’ would need replacing by ‘such that it reaches’ to exclude formal corruption. It therefore defines investigation generally, yet the premises may be neither known nor believed but instances of compound ignorance, which it fails to include.”

Investigation is also defined as considering what is intellectually apprehended to acquire what is unknown. “Intellectually apprehended” means whatever is present to the intellect, one thing or several, conception or assent, knowledge, opinion or compound ignorance. None of the preceding strained qualifications is then needed.

title: Intellectual attention and the analogy of vision
en:
The Imām says that inward vision closely resembles outward vision. Someone seeking to see a thing turns his gaze away from other things and moves his eye from side to side until it faces the object and sees it. Likewise, someone seeking intellectual apprehension turns away from other things and moves the eye of his intellect from one thing to another until he obtains the ordered cognitions leading to the object sought.

Accordingly, investigation is described as clearing the mind of distractions: emptying it of diversions and preoccupations obstructing the radiance of the divine light that causes the sought object to flow into it. Or it is described as directing the intellect's gaze toward intelligibles, seeking what prepares it for that influx.

Since investigation is plainly distinguished from the soul's other movements by its end—so plainly that every definition indicates that end—the theologians define it as thought through which knowledge or opinion is sought. “Thought” means the soul's movement among meanings. Specifying meanings excludes imaginative movement. As the commentary on the *Ishārāt* explains, thought may name any movement of the soul, through the faculty whose instrument is the front of the brain's middle ventricle, provided that it concerns intelligibles. Movement concerning sensibles may instead be called imagination.

The *Mawāqif*'s explanation in terms of imaginative movements is therefore unsuitable. The commentary on legal theory is correct: thought is the soul's intentional passage among meanings. “Intentional” apparently excludes intuition and its other unintentional movements. Thought is thus like a genus of investigation. As the Imām of the Two Sanctuaries says, thought may seek knowledge or opinion and then be called investigation; or it may not, as with much inner conversation.

title: Why the definition includes thought and opinion
en:
Al-Āmidī's objection therefore falls: that “thought” is redundant because the rest of the definition suffices. He defends the wording by saying that thought is not part of the definition: it is as though one said, “Investigation is thought, and thought is what seeks knowledge or opinion.” This is acceptable insofar as thought in familiar usage is virtually synonymous with investigation, rather than broader, so defining it by seeking knowledge or opinion is possible. But the interpretation is remote from the actual wording and unlike normal definitions. One does not, for example, define a human as “a man, who is a rational animal.” Moreover, “that through which knowledge or opinion is sought” does not itself adequately explain either investigation or thought without strain.

His further objection is that opinion may fail to correspond and thus be ignorance, which cannot be sought. The reply is that what is sought is opinion as opinion; this does not entail seeking the narrower case, noncorresponding opinion, and therefore does not entail seeking ignorance.

The judge Abū Bakr's wording is “knowledge or predominance of opinion.” It is objected that this excludes investigation seeking opinion itself. Al-Āmidī answers that seeking knowledge, seeking opinion and seeking its predominance are each properties of investigation, and a definition may mention only some properties. The *Mawāqif* replies that this is permissible only for a property encompassing every instance, whereas none of the three does. Hence “seeking knowledge” alone is insufficient because it excludes seeking opinion. When each defining property covers only some divisions, all must be included in a division, producing an encompassing property: having one of these characteristics. “Or” states the divisions of the defined thing, not ambiguity or hesitation incompatible with definition.

He then answers that opinion itself is called “predominance of opinion,” because predominance belongs to its reality: it is the preponderant belief. This excuse is unclear. The predominance of a judgement within opinion's reality does not itself justify or motivate calling opinion the predominance of opinion—unless the genitive means the predominance characteristic of opinion, rather than attributing predominance to opinion as its agent.

It is also said that each of the three properties encompasses every instance. Actual pursuit of knowledge or opinion is not intended; rather, thought must be of a kind suited to it, moving among intelligibles to obtain the object's principles. The thought by which knowledge is sought is also that by which opinion or its predominance is sought. It would then be permissible to mention only one.

title: Second investigation: the matter and form of reasoning
en:
His words “the second investigation” introduce the following. Whether investigation is the arrangement itself or the movement leading to it, it requires cognitions ordered in a specific configuration. What leads to conception is called a defining account; what leads to assent, a proof. The cognitions—that is, the matters present to the mind—are the matter of this means of reaching the object, and the resulting configuration is its form. Matter and form may also be attributed to investigation because of this connection, or because thought and investigation are used for the ordered cognitions, as in the Imām's wording. This is the meaning of the *Mawāqif*'s statement that every arrangement has matter and form.

Some commonly identify the form with the arrangement. Investigators, however, distinguish them: arrangement is the parts' standing in a certain disposition toward one another, or placing them in it; form is the configuration accruing to the parts after arrangement, through which they are called one.

All agree that if matter and form are sound, investigation is sound and leads to the object sought; otherwise it is defective and does not lead to it. In a defining account, sound matter requires that what is given as genus really be the quiddity's genus, what is given as differentia really be its differentia, and what is given as a distinctive property be an encompassing concomitant. A complete definition must include proximate genus and differentia, and other conditions must also be met. In a proof, the premises must suit the object sought and be true with certainty, probability or by supposition, according to the aims described in the five logical disciplines.

Sound form in a defining account requires putting the more general first and restricting it by the differentia or distinctive property, producing one form corresponding to or distinguishing the object sought. In a proof, it requires the conditions governing consequence, as detailed in logic's discussions of syllogism, induction and analogy.

It follows that dividing investigation into sound and defective according to matter and form involves transferred usage. There is therefore no difficulty in similarly dividing it into evident and obscure. The parts of a defining account or proof may be immediate yet differ in clarity; or inferential, terminating in immediate knowledge through fewer or more intermediaries. Syllogistic figures likewise differ in form. The *Mawāqif*'s wording may suggest that transferred usage applies only to the evident/obscure division and only to proof, not defining accounts, and that the sound/defective division according to matter and form depends upon defining investigation as arrangement.

title: Does sound investigation yield certainty?
en:
**He says:** “Sound investigation, together with its conditions…”

The Imām says that no one disputes investigation's yielding opinion; the dispute concerns certainty. The Sumaniyya deny that it yields certainty at all, and some philosophers deny it in divine science and natural philosophy. Aristotle is even reported to have said that certainty cannot be attained in divine investigations: their highest possible aim is to adopt what is more appropriate and fitting. This narrower issue is more plausible as the point of dispute, since no uncertainty is conceivable about two multiplied by two yielding four.

In general, the Imām, seeking to refute the deniers, confines himself to establishing that some investigation yields knowledge, whether generally or concerning divine matters. Al-Āmidī, seeking a rule applying to the particular sound investigations through which we acquire knowledge, needs a universal affirmative proposition. He therefore restricts investigation to certain matters, since probabilistic investigation admittedly does not yield knowledge, and excludes its being followed by sleep, inattention, death or another contrary of apprehension. In those circumstances neither knowledge nor even opinion occurs. Each is treated as a contrary of apprehension according to the theologians, even if this differs from the philosophers' terminology.

We omit restriction to certain matters because “sound” makes it unnecessary. Investigation from probabilistic matter in pursuit of knowledge is materially defective, since its matter does not suit its object. The omission also includes investigation seeking conception. Nevertheless, theologians' unqualified use of “knowledge” and “investigation” apparently concerns assent. Our inclusion of both conception and assent in their definitions—knowledge as an attribute yielding discrimination admitting no contrary, and investigation as thought seeking knowledge or opinion—thus involves some interpretive extension on our part.

title: Customary succession, acquisition and generated effects
en:
**He says:** “In the sense of its occurring after it.”

This indicates how investigation yields knowledge. On our account, God creates knowledge after investigation is completed, in the customary course: this happens repeatedly and consistently without being necessary, since God may exceptionally refrain from creating it. As will be explained, all contingent things depend immediately upon God's power and choice; an effect of a choosing agent is not necessary [in the sense excluded here].

Those holding this position divide into two groups. Some attribute the knowledge solely to beginningless power, without the servant's power relating to it. The servant's power concerns only bringing the two premises to mind and considering the conclusion's potential presence within them. Others make the knowledge itself acquired and subject to the servant's power.

For the Muʿtazilites it occurs through generation: one act necessitates another act for the same agent, as the hand's movement produces the key's movement. Investigation, however explained, is an act of the investigator that produces another act of his, knowledge. “Act” here means the effect resulting from an agent, not the exercise of influence itself. The objection that knowledge is not an act, and neither is investigation on most definitions, is therefore misplaced. Movement is likewise not an act in that narrower sense, yet all agree that the hand's and key's movements are two acts of one agent.

Some of our companions, after refuting generation generally, argue against it here: recalling an investigation admittedly does not generate knowledge; neither, therefore, does investigating initially, since both share the character of investigation.

It is objected that this does not yield certainty: it returns to juridical analogy, even if cast as a logical syllogism—“If investigation generated knowledge, recollecting it would do so because there is no relevant difference; but the consequent is admittedly false.” Nor does it bind the opponents. They deny generation in the original case, recollection, for a reason absent from the new case, initial investigation: involuntary recollection lies outside the servant's power and choice. Deliberate recollection would generate knowledge.

This is therefore a composite analogy: the proponent and opponent agree upon the original case's ruling but explain it by different causes. The opponent can deny the common feature—initial investigation does not share involuntary recollection's absence of control—or deny the ruling when recollection is voluntary. Only recollection arising without intention is God's act; if knowledge were generated from it, that too would be God's act, and obliging the servant to perform it would be inappropriate.

The *Nihāyat al-ʿuqūl* suggests another reason why recollection does not generate knowledge: two necessitating factors would converge upon one effect. Recollection comprises two cognitions: knowledge of the preceding premises and knowledge that one previously possessed those cognitions. Neither is more entitled than the other to generate the conclusion, so each would generate the same knowledge, which is impossible. Alternatively, the reason may be that it would produce what is already obtained: recollection follows investigation, which has already produced knowledge. On this explanation, recollection yields no new knowledge at all.

Recollection comprises two cognitions: knowledge of the preceding premises and knowledge that one previously possessed those cognitions. Neither is more entitled than the other to generate the conclusion, so each would generate the same knowledge, which is impossible. Alternatively, the reason may be that it would produce what is already obtained: recollection follows investigation, which has already produced knowledge. On this explanation, recollection yields no new knowledge at all.

title: The philosophers' explanation and rational entailment
en:
For the philosophers, knowledge follows necessarily because the recipient is fully prepared and the agent remains continuously active. Investigation prepares the mind for knowledge's influx from the Giver of Forms. In their view this is the Active Intellect, bearing the forms of beings and imparting them to our souls according to their readiness when they connect with it. They claim that the Preserved Tablet and Clear Book in religious language are names for this intellect.

There is another position, chosen by the Imām al-Rāzī, which the Proof of Islam, al-Ghazālī, says most of our companions hold: investigation entails knowledge of the conclusion through unavoidable necessity, but not through generation as the Muʿtazilites maintain. This is the view transmitted from the judge Abū Bakr and the Imām of the Two Sanctuaries: investigation necessarily entails knowledge without being its cause or generator. Necessity is expressly stated so that “entailment” is not interpreted as customary succession, which would reduce this to the first position. Al-Ghazālī explicitly attributes this view to most of our companions, and the first to some.

Al-Rāzī argues for necessity: someone who knows that the world changes and that everything changing is contingent cannot, while both cognitions are present, fail to know that the world is contingent. This impossibility is immediately known. The same applies to every consequent together with what entails it. He argues against generation that knowledge is intrinsically contingent and therefore within God's power; it cannot occur independently of that power.

The *Mawāqif* objects: being the act of a powerful agent excludes necessity. Such an agent acts if He wills and refrains if He wills, with no necessity imposed upon Him or issuing from Him. One cannot answer that the necessity is through choice, as will be explained later: in that case the effect may fail to occur because power and choice do not relate to it, returning exactly to the first position.

The reply is that the necessity of an effect such as knowledge, meaning its inseparability from another effect such as investigation, does not conflict with its being an effect of a choosing agent who may act or refrain. He may refrain by creating neither knowledge nor what entails it, not by creating what entails it without creating the knowledge. The same applies to other contingent correlates, such as substance's existence accompanying an accident's existence.

More precisely, the possibility of refraining includes refraining with or without an intermediary. The possibility of omitting something within one's power may depend upon removing an obstacle that is itself within one's power. Generated effects are like this for those Muʿtazilites who attribute them to the servant's power. What conflicts with choice is an effect's inseparability from the agent such that the agent cannot refrain from it at all.

If the objection succeeded, all relations of entailment between contingent things would disappear. Conceiving a son would not entail conceiving a father, and an accident's existence would not entail a substance's existence, and so forth. In short, these scholars regard knowledge's entailment by investigation as rationally inseparable, like the conception of father entailed by conception of son. The first group regards it as customary, allowing exceptional separation, like burning associated with fire. The matn indicates our companions' three positions by saying: customarily, with acquisition or without it, or through rational entailment.

title: Can reasoning establish its own reliability?
en:
**He says:** “If it is said…”

The objection is this. The judgement that investigation yields knowledge is either immediate or inferential, and both alternatives are false. If immediate, reasonable people would not disagree about it, just as they do not disagree about other immediate cognitions; and it would be as clear as “one is half of two.” Degrees of clarity indicate uncertainty and ambiguity, incompatible with immediacy. Yet disagreement occurs and differences in clarity are evident.

If inferential, it must be established by investigation. This produces circularity because it depends upon the proof and upon the proof's entailing its conclusion, which is precisely its yielding knowledge. It also produces contradiction: it is known insofar as it serves as a means, and unknown insofar as it is sought. This is what is meant by saying that establishing investigation through investigation is contradictory.

If it is said: “Establishing an inferential proposition means obtaining knowledge of it through investigation: one knows the ordered premises and thereby knows the conclusion. This depends only upon investigation's actually yielding knowledge, not upon knowing that it does. What depends is assent; what is depended upon is truth. Similarly, conceiving a quiddity is obtained through its inseparable distinctive property: conceiving the property yields conception of the quiddity, even without knowing exclusivity or entailment.”

We answer: the argument assumes that, in a syllogism, the truth of the conclusion is entailed and the truth of the ordered premises entails it. Assent to the conclusion—knowing its truth—is entailed by assent to the ordered premises **and** to their entailing the object sought, whether immediately or by acquisition. As established, knowledge that a consequent obtains is acquired from knowledge of the entailment and knowledge that the antecedent obtains. Definition through a distinctive property differs: there, entailment holds between the two conceptions themselves. If assent to the premises and assent to the conclusion stood in that same relation, the objection would fall.

title: Immediate recognition and a particular proof
en:
The answer may choose the immediate alternative. We deny that disagreement and differing clarity are impossible among immediate cognitions. A group of reasonable people may disagree because the conceptions of the terms are obscure or difficult to separate from accompanying features that prevent the judgement from becoming evident. Degrees of clarity may arise from differences in these respects and in the frequency with which the soul attends to the propositions.

Alternatively, we choose the inferential alternative: the claim is established through a particular investigation whose premises and consequence are immediately evident, without circularity or contradiction. Take “the world changes, and everything changing is temporally originated.” This particular arrangement, or these ordered cognitions, is investigation, since investigation means nothing else. It immediately yields knowledge that the world is temporally originated. Therefore some investigation yields knowledge, which is the Imām's claim.

If we wish to establish al-Āmidī's universal rule, we add: it is immediately known that this result does not arise from the peculiar matter of this instance, but from the investigation's sound matter and form and fulfilment of its conditions. Every investigation meeting these requirements therefore yields knowledge.

This is what the Imām of the Two Sanctuaries means when he says that there is no difficulty in establishing all kinds of investigation through one kind that establishes itself and the others. Because he acknowledged something's establishing itself, al-Rāzī objected that this involves contradiction and a thing's priority to itself.

The reply is that what is intrinsically the same may differ in consideration and therefore in its judgements. The investigation through which we establish that every investigation yields judgement is, in itself, a known and prior means; considered as an instance of investigation generally, it is a posterior and unknown object sought.

title: A singular case is not the universal proposition
en:
More precisely, what depends, is unknown and is sought through investigation is an unquantified or universally quantified affirmative proposition whose subject is the concept of investigation: “investigation yields knowledge,” or “every investigation accompanied by its conditions yields knowledge.” What it depends upon, immediately known, is a singular proposition whose subject is this particular investigation: “the world changes, and everything changing is temporally originated, yields knowledge that the world is temporally originated.” This is known without considering that subject as an instance of investigation generally. Therefore something identical both intrinsically and in consideration is not prior to itself, or known while unknown; circularity and contradiction do not follow.

The fundamental point is that predicating something of a subject may differ in its requirements—whether it needs no proof, needs proof, needs a reminder, needs sensation or something else—according to how the subject is expressed. Seeking to predicate temporal origination of the world, we may express it in a way that conveys nothing new: “everything existing after nonexistence is temporally originated”; or something informative and self-evident: “everything accompanying the connection of originated power and will is temporally originated”; or something informative and acquired: “everything changing is temporally originated.”

This also resolves the objection to the first figure: knowing the conclusion depends upon knowing the universal major premise, whose subject's instances include the conclusion's subject; therefore the conclusion supposedly depends upon itself and is known before being known. But knowing the judgement—for example, the world's temporal origination—under the aspect of the subject's being an instance of the middle term, “changing,” does not conflict with its being unknown under the aspect of the minor term, “world.”

title: Syllogistic figures and awareness of consequence
en:
If it is said: “Investigation's yielding knowledge is plainly immediate in the first figure and inferential in the other figures. How can al-Rāzī call it immediate without qualification, or the Imām of the Two Sanctuaries inferential without qualification?”

We answer: the dispute concerns the proposition whose subject is investigation generally: “investigation,” or “every investigation fulfilling its conditions,” yields knowledge. The stated distinction concerns particular instances, such as “the world changes” together with “everything changing is temporally originated,” or together with “nothing beginningless changes.” Knowledge that the first yields its conclusion is immediate; knowledge that the second does so is inferential.

Moreover, that distinction considers only the arrangement of the premises and the middle term's position relative to the other terms. Once all conditions are present, the judgement that each particular investigation yields knowledge is immediate in every figure, according to some investigators. They include among the conditions awareness of how the premises indicate the conclusion and how it is potentially contained within them.

The Imām, the Proof of Islam, calls this the specific cause of the conclusion's actual occurrence. Without it, one may overlook the conclusion although both premises are present. Someone seeing a mule with a swollen belly may suppose it pregnant while recognising that it is a mule and that every mule is barren. Once the mode of consequence and the conclusion's containment are noticed, all figures are equally clear. Some investigators even say that all then reduce intellectually to the first figure, although one may be unable to formulate the expression accordingly. The author of the *Mawāqif* fully examines this in his commentary on legal theory.

title: Is noticing the conclusion's containment an additional premise?
en:
The scholars maintain that awareness of this containment is immediately known to be a condition of obtaining the conclusion; the mule example merely draws attention to it. The Imām's denial—that such a mistake occurs only when one premise is present, and that once both are combined uncertainty about the conclusion is impossible—is obstinate.

His argument against the condition is weak: if containment were something known in addition to the two premises, it would be another premise required for consequence. One must then ask how it combines with the first two, producing an infinite regress of premises. But what is intended is consideration of the premises' relation to the conclusion, not a proposition constituting part of the syllogism and thus a premise. Even if it is called a premise or explained as assent that the minor term is among the middle term's instances of which the major is universally predicated, it need not form with the two premises another configuration whose containment must be known, requiring a fourth premise and so on.

If it is said: “No one disputes that the premises' bare presence is insufficient. They must have a specific arrangement, the formal component, placing them in a valid mood. Moreover, outside the first figure, entailment must be explained through reduction to absurdity, conversion or the like. Even if the mule example's premises were present in the fourth figure, uncertainty could remain until their order was reversed. What, then, is disputed?”

We answer: whether knowledge of the conclusion, after the syllogism is complete in matter and form—that is, the premises are present in a valid configuration—requires attending to that configuration, the conclusion's relation to them and its potential containment within them. In the first figure this occurs by mere attention; in the others, through acquisition. All return to showing that an affirmation or negation serving as intermediary entails the affirmation or negation sought, which is the reality of the first figure. The various methods of proof would serve to obtain this condition.

title: Logical entailment and knowing that entailment
en:
Some later scholars therefore argue for this condition from the figures' differing clarity in yielding conclusions. They do not regard the argument as decisive: the methods of proof may not merely produce awareness of containment, but may themselves be conditions for knowing the entailment of conclusions by the figures. Some entailments are known immediately; others through an obscure or still more obscure intermediary.

The argument is sometimes presented thus: the same two premises may form a figure with evident consequence—“the world changes; everything changing is temporally originated”—or one with less evident consequence, reversing their order: “everything changing is temporally originated; the world changes.” If configuration played no role in entailment, this difference would not arise, since the matter is the same.

The answer is that the consequents differ: “the world is temporally originated,” and “some temporally originated thing is the world.” One consequent's entailment may be clearer even when the antecedent is the same. If the consequent is kept fixed as “the world is temporally originated,” deriving it through another figure requires changing one or both premises. The third figure gives “some changing thing is the world; everything changing is temporally originated”; the fourth may use “every temporally originated thing changes,” if the conversion is universally true. The matter then differs, and one entailment may be clearer. Once the precise dispute has been established, you can assess this formulation yourself.

One cannot argue that differing figures conclusively establish the condition: a syllogism fulfilling its conditions necessarily entails its conclusion, and a consequent cannot fail to accompany a complete antecedent. Unless awareness of containment were a condition attained differently—by attention in some cases, through more or less obscure intermediaries in others—all valid moods would equally produce their conclusions when present.

We answer: a thing's following necessarily differs from knowing that it follows. All valid moods and figures equally entail their conclusions in the sense that the conclusions are true in reality if the premises are true. The difference concerns knowing this. Its conditions—attention or acquisition through more or less obscure means—may be attained differently, even if awareness of containment is not itself one of those conditions.

title: Six objections to knowledge through investigation
en:
**He says:** “The opponent argues in several ways.”

We did not include the preceding doubt among them because these arguments deny that the assent following investigation is knowledge, either generally, in natural and divine science, or in divine science alone. This follows the Imām's statement that investigation's yielding opinion is undisputed, whereas its yielding complete certainty is disputed. Arithmetic should not be included in that dispute. The preceding doubt, by contrast, denies that investigation yields assent at all.

The first objection: if knowing that the belief arising after investigation is knowledge is immediate, the opposite could neither occur after investigation nor become apparent later, since what contradicts immediate knowledge can neither occur nor become evident. Yet many people obtain only ignorance from their investigations, and investigators often later discover the opposite, recognise their mistake and change schools. If such knowing is inferential, another investigation is required to establish that it is knowledge, producing an infinite regress.

The reply may choose the immediate alternative. We deny that the opposite occurs through or after the investigation in question, because the discussion concerns sound investigation: truth's consequence is certainly true. Or we choose the inferential alternative but deny that another investigation is needed. The same sound investigation yields both knowledge of the conclusion and knowledge that this is knowledge rather than ignorance or opinion.

The same applies to knowing that there is no opposing argument: no genuine opposition to sound investigation in certain matters is conceivable. This removes another doubt: “If investigation yields knowledge, one must know there is no opponent, since opposition prevents firmness. Such knowledge is not immediate, because opposing arguments often appear. It therefore requires another investigation, itself dependent upon the absence of opposition, and so on without end.”

Thus the phrase “like knowledge that there is no opposing argument” means that this may be immediate, and we deny that a genuine opponent appears after sound investigation; or inferential, and we deny that it depends upon another investigation. There is a further issue here, which we shall disclose at the division's end.

The *Ṭawāliʿ*'s formulation is deficient: “The knowledge resulting from investigation is either immediate or inferential, and both are impossible.” An expression must be supplied: the knowledge-character of that cognition—its being knowledge. Only then can one legitimately choose the immediate alternative. Otherwise, what results through investigation is not immediate, except in the sense that we are compelled to assent because we assent to the premises; in that sense, immediacy is not opposed to inferential cognition.

title: Inquiry requires not yet knowing its conclusion
en:
The second objection: investigation is conditioned by absence of knowledge of its object, lest one seek what is already obtained. If it yielded knowledge, meaning that it entailed knowledge rationally or customarily, it could not be conditioned by that knowledge's absence: an antecedent cannot be conditioned by the absence of its consequent.

The answer is that entailment here means rational or customary succession: knowledge of the object must occur when investigation is completed. What entails knowledge is investigation's completion; what is conditioned by absence of knowledge is its continuation.

The answer is that entailment here means rational or customary succession: knowledge of the object must occur when investigation is completed. What entails knowledge is investigation's completion; what is conditioned by absence of knowledge is its continuation.

title: Obligation, choice and inferential knowledge
en:
The third objection: if investigation yielded knowledge in the sense of its necessarily following rationally or customarily, imposing knowledge as an obligation would be wrong. It would resemble immediate knowledge in lying outside power and choice and in not grounding entitlement to reward or punishment.

Even conceding the principle of rational wrongness, the answer is that obligation concerns acts, not qualities, relations or passive affections. According to investigators, knowledge is a quality, not an act. The obligation therefore concerns acquiring it by undertaking its means, such as directing one's faculty, investigating and employing distinctive properties.

This must be what al-Āmidī means when he says that obligation concerns investigation, which is within one's power, rather than the object investigated. Otherwise the obligation to know the Maker, His oneness and similar matters is unmistakable. In sum, inferential knowledge can be acquired or left unacquired, unlike immediate knowledge. Its necessarily following completed investigation does not conflict with this. For the same reason, the contradictory of an inferential proposition can be believed, whereas that of a self-evident proposition cannot [in the sense at issue].

title: Difficulty is not impossibility
en:
The fourth objection: the thing nearest and most intimately connected with a human being is his identity, indicated by “I.” Yet great disagreement surrounds it. Investigation has not established with certainty whether it is this sensible bodily structure, subtle parts permeating it, an indivisible part in the heart, an immaterial substance connected with the body, or something else. How, then, could investigation establish more remote things: the heavens, elements and wonders of composite bodies; or still more remote things, immaterial beings and divine questions concerning essence and attributes?

The answer is that this shows only the difficulty of acquiring such knowledge through investigation, not its impossibility. The dispute concerns impossibility, not difficulty.

title: Is exhaustive conception of divine realities required?
en:
The fifth objection: if investigation yielded knowledge, that is assent, concerning divine realities, its prerequisite, conception, would have to be present. But it is not present immediately; nor can it be acquired. A definition is impossible because composition is impossible [in the realities concerned], while a description does not supply conception of the reality.

The answer is that a description may supply a conception of the reality, even though it does not invariably do so. Even granting the objection, conception under some aspect is sufficient.

title: A proof does not bring its object into existence
en:
The sixth objection: knowledge of the Necessary's existence is the foundation of divine science and cannot be acquired through investigation. Acquisition requires a proof yielding and indicating something. This must be either the Maker's establishedness itself or knowledge of Him; otherwise it would not prove Him.

If it is the former, absence of the proof entails the Maker's absence, since absence of what produces something entails absence of what is produced. If it is the latter, failure to investigate the proof entails its not being a proof, since proofhood is a relative attribute existing only in relation to the indicated thing, here assumed to be knowledge, which is absent without investigation.

We answer: saying that a proof yields or necessitates something does not mean that it brings it into existence and produces it, as causes do. It means that whenever the proof exists, that thing exists, and whenever the proof is investigated, that thing becomes known. In short, the proof's existence entails the object's establishedness, and investigating the proof entails knowledge of the object. Absence of an antecedent plainly does not entail absence of its consequent. Nor does failure to investigate a proof conflict with its being such that, when investigated, its object becomes known.

title: The self-defeat of a universal argument against reasoning
en:
An objection applies to all these arguments—indeed, to any argument that investigation does not yield knowledge. Is knowledge of that claim inferential, obtained through one of the arguments? Then contradiction follows, since some investigation has yielded knowledge. Or is it immediate, the arguments merely reminders? Then most reasonable people oppose an immediate judgement, which is immediately known to be false. What is possible is disagreement by some reasonable people; that does not entail the possibility of disagreement by the majority.

If they say: “We acknowledge that argument yields no knowledge. But because you argued that it does, we countered with an argument that it does not, opposing one invalid argument with another.”

We answer: if your arguments establish that ours are invalid, investigation yields knowledge, as required. If they establish nothing, they are idle and our argument remains unopposed.
